Tafsir (commentary) of Surat as-Saffat. It is Meccan, according to the consensus of all scholars.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

By those ranged in ranks (1), then those who drive with a driving (2), then those who recite the reminder (3), indeed your God is One (4), Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and Lord of the easts (5).

God, the Exalted, says: ﴿By those ranged in ranks. Then those who drive with a driving. Then those who recite the reminder﴾. This is the recitation of the majority of the reciters (qurra'). Hamzah recited it with idgham (assimilation of the letters) in all three. This is the recitation that Ahmad ibn Hanbal disliked when he heard it. An-Nahhas said: It is weak in Arabic from three aspects. First, the letter ta' (ت) does not share the articulation point of sad (ص), nor of zay (ز), nor of dhal (ذ), nor of their counterparts. Its counterparts are ta' and dal (د) for the letter ta', sad and sin (س) for the letter zay, and za' (ظ) and tha' (ث) for the letter dhal. Second, the ta' is in one word and what follows it is in another word. Third, if you assimilate, you bring together two sukun letters (unvocalized consonants) from two words. Bringing together two sukun letters in such a case is permissible only when they are within one word, as in dabbah and shabbah. The justification for Hamzah's recitation is that the ta' is close in articulation to these letters.

Wa-s-saffat (وَالصَّافَّاتِ, "by those ranged in ranks") is an oath. The wa (و) replaces the ba' (ب) of oath, so the meaning is "by the Lord of those ranged in ranks." Fa-z-zajirat (فَالزَّاجِراتِ) is coordinated with it (ʿatf). Inna ilahakum lawahid (إِنَّ إِلهَكُمْ لَواحِدٌ, "indeed your God is One") is the answer to the oath. Al-Kisa'i permitted opening inna (أَنَّ) after an oath.

What is meant by "those ranged in ranks" and what follows up to His words "those who recite the reminder" is the angels, according to the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Masʿud, ʿIkrimah, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, and Qatadah. They are arranged in rows in the heaven as people are arranged in rows in this world for prayer. It is also said: they spread their wings in the air, standing in it until God commands them with what He wills. This is like servants standing before their kings in rows. Al-Hasan said: "ranged in ranks" refers to their rows before their Lord in their prayer. It is also said that they are birds, and the evidence for this is His words: ﴿Have they not seen the birds above them, spreading their wings?﴾ [al-Mulk: 19]. Al-Saff (الصَّفُّ) is the arrangement of a group along a line, like the rows in prayer. Al-Saffat (الصَّافَّاتِ) is a plural of plural: one says jama'ah saffah (جَمَاعَةٌ صَافَّةٌ, "a group ranged"), then it is pluralized as saffat (صَافَّاتٍ). It is also said: al-Saffat are the groups of believing people when they stand in rows in prayer or in jihad, as mentioned by al-Qushayri.

Fa-z-zajirat (فَالزَّاجِراتِ) are the angels, according to the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Masʿud, Masruq, and others, as we have mentioned. This is either because they drive the clouds and herd them, according to al-Suddi, or because they drive people away from sins through admonitions and advice. Qatadah said: they are the admonitions of the Qur'an.

Fa-t-taliyat dhikran (فَالتَّالِياتِ ذِكْراً, "those who recite the reminder") are the angels who recite the Book of God, according to Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, and al-Suddi. It is also said that what is meant is Jibril alone, but he is mentioned in the plural form because he is the chief of the angels and is never without troops and followers. Qatadah said: what is meant is everyone who recites the remembrance of God and His books. It is also said that they are the verses of the Qur'an, and it described them with recitation as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an relates to the Children of Israel﴾ [an-Naml: 76]. It is permissible to say that the verses of the Qur'an are "reciters," because some letters follow others, as mentioned by al-Qushayri. Al-Mawardi mentioned that what is meant by "those who recite" is the prophets who recite the reminder to their nations.

If it is asked: what is the function of fa (فَ) when it comes as a coordinating particle among descriptions? It is said to him: it either indicates the sequence of its meanings in existence, as in the statement of [[He is Salamah ibn Dhuhl, known as Ibn Zayyabah, and Zayyabah is his father. It is also said it is the name of his mother. He says: "Alas my father for al-Harith when my people are attacked at dawn, and he takes booty and returns safe. Would that I had met him and killed him." He means "alas for my self." Al-Harith is al-Harith ibn Hammam al-Shaybani, as in the commentary on the poems of al-Hamasah. After this line:

"By God, if I had met him alone, and he returned with us driving camels among the victors."]]:

Alas for Zayyabah's sake, for al-Harith, the one who attacks at dawn, the one who takes booty, the one who returns.

As if he said: the one who attacked at dawn, then took booty, then returned. Or it indicates their order in terms of gradation in some respects, as in your saying: "Take the best, then the most perfect, and do the finest, then the most beautiful." Or it indicates the order of their referents in that, as in His saying: "May God have mercy on those who shave their heads, then those who trim them." On these three principles the function of the coordinating fa in descriptions is explained, as al-Zamakhshari said.

"Indeed your God is One" is the answer to the oath. Muqatil said: this is because the disbelievers in Mecca said: "Has he made the gods into one god? How can a single god encompass this creation!" So God swore by these in honor.

Then the verse was revealed. Ibn al-Anbari said: this is a good place to pause, and then one begins with "Lord of the heavens and the earth," meaning "He is the Lord of the heavens." An-Nahhas said: it is permissible for "Lord of the heavens and the earth" to be a predicate after a predicate, and it is permissible for it to be an apposition (badal) to "One." I say: on these two aspects, one does not pause at "lawahid" (One). Al-Akhfash related: "Rabba as-samawati wa-rabba al-mashariq" (رَبَّ السَّمَوَاتِ وَرَبَّ الْمَشَارِقِ) in the accusative, as a qualifier of the noun of inna.

He, glorified be He, explained the meaning of His oneness, His divinity, and the perfection of His power by saying that He is "Lord of the heavens and the earth," that is, their Creator and Owner, "and what is between them, and Lord of the easts," that is, the Owner of the places where the sun rises. Ibn ʿAbbas said: the sun has a rising point and a setting point every day. God created for the sun three hundred and sixty-five openings at its rising point, and the same number at its setting point, according to the number of days of the solar year. It rises each day from one of them and sets in another. It does not rise from that opening except on that day of the following year. It rises only while unwilling, and it says: "My Lord, do not make me rise over Your servants, for I see them disobeying You." This was mentioned by Abu ʿUmar in the book at-Tamhid, and by Ibn al-Anbari in the book ar-Radd, from ʿIkrimah, who said: I said to Ibn ʿAbbas: "What do you think of what came from the Prophet (ﷺ) about Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt: 'His poetry believed, but his heart disbelieved'?" He said: "It is true. What have you denied of that?" I said: "We denied his saying:"

The sun rises every last night, and the reddish one, its color turns rosy at dawn.

It does not rise upon them in its course, except tormented, and except flogged.

"Why is the sun flogged?" He said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, the sun never rises until seventy thousand angels prod it. They say to it: 'Rise, rise.' It says: 'I will not rise upon a people who worship me besides God.' Then an angel comes to it and deems the light of the children of Adam insufficient. Then a devil comes to it, wanting to block it from rising, so it rises between his two horns, and God burns him beneath it." That is the saying of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "It only rises between the two horns of a devil, and it only sets between the two horns of a devil, and it never sets except that it falls prostrate before God. Then a devil comes to it, wanting to prevent it from prostrating, so it sets between his two horns, and God burns him beneath it." This is the wording of Ibn al-Anbari. He also mentioned from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) told the truth about Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt in this poem:"

Zuhal and Thawr are beneath its right foot, and the eagle for the other, and a lion lies in wait.

And the sun rises every last night, and the reddish one, its color turns rosy at dawn.

It does not rise upon them in its course, except tormented, and except flogged.

ʿIkrimah said: I said to Ibn ʿAbbas: "O my master, is the sun flogged?" He said: "The rhyme forced him to say 'flogged,' but it fears punishment."

By mentioning the rising points, he indicated the setting points, so he did not mention the setting points. This is like His saying: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [an-Nahl: 81]. He singled out the rising points for mention because sunrise comes before sunset. In Surat ar-Rahman He said: ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾ [ar-Rahman: 17]. By "the two easts" He meant the furthest rising point from which the sun rises on the longest days, and the shortest day among the shortest days, as was mentioned earlier in Surat Ya-Sin [[See p. 27 and following of this part.]]. And God knows best.

**Qur'an 37:6–10**

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, We have adorned the nearest heaven with an adornment, the stars﴾. Qatadah said: The stars were created for three purposes: as missiles against the devils (shayatin), as a light by which people are guided, and as an adornment for the lowest heaven.

Masruq, al-A'mash, al-Nakha'i, Asim and Hamzah read *bi-zinatin* (with kasra and tanwin) and *al-kawakib* in the genitive (*khufida*), as a *badal* (apposition, substitution) for *bi-zinatin*, because the stars are themselves the adornment. Abu Bakr read it the same way, except that he put *al-kawakiba* in the accusative (*nasaba*), governed by the verbal noun *zinah*. The meaning is: "by adorning the stars in it." It is also permissible for it to be accusative by an implied verb *a'ni* (I mean), as if he said: "We adorned it with an adornment, namely the stars." It was also said that it is an apposition to *zinah* by way of its position (*'ala al-mahall*).

It is also permissible to read *bi-zinatin al-kawakib* with the meaning that its adornment is the stars, or with the meaning "they are the stars." The rest of the readers read *bi-zinati al-kawakib* as a genitive construction (*idafah*). The meaning is: "We adorned the lowest heaven by the adornment of the stars," that is, by the beauty of the stars. It is also permissible that it is like the reading of those who read with tanwin, except that the tanwin is omitted for lightness.

*Wa-hifzan* is a verbal noun (*masdar*), meaning: "We guarded it, a guarding." ﴿And as protection from every rebellious devil﴾. When He informed that the angels descend with revelation from the heaven, He explained that He guarded the heaven against eavesdropping (*istiraq al-sam'*) after adorning it with the stars. *Al-marid* is the one who is stubborn and defiant among the jinn and humans, and the Arabs call him a *shaytan*.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They cannot listen to the exalted assembly﴾. Abu Hatim said: That is, "so that they do not hear," then the *an* was dropped and the verb became *raf'*-ed. *Al-Mala' al-A'la* (the exalted assembly): the people of the lowest heaven and what is above it. All of them are called "exalted" in relation to the assembly of the earth. The pronoun in *yassamma'una* refers to the devils. The majority of people read *yasma'una* with a sukun on the *sin* and a light *mim*. Hamzah and Asim, in the narration of Hafs, read *la yassamma'una* with a shaddah on the *sin* and the *mim*, from *tasmi'* (causing to hear). According to the first reading, their hearing is negated even if they listen, and this is the correct meaning, supported by Allah's saying: ﴿Indeed, they are removed from the hearing﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 212]. According to the last reading, any listening or hearing from them is negated. Mujahid said: They used to try to eavesdrop, but they did not hear. It is narrated from Ibn Abbas that about *la yassamma'una ila al-mala'*, he said: They do not hear and they do not try to eavesdrop.

The original form of *yassamma'una* is *yatasamma'una*, and the *ta'* was assimilated into the *sin* (*idgham*, assimilation) because they are close in articulation. Abu Ubayd preferred this, because the Arabs hardly say *sami'tu ilayhi* (I heard to him), while they say *tasamma'tu ilayhi* (I listened attentively to him).

﴿And they are pelted from every side﴾, that is, they are struck from every side, namely with meteors (*shuhub*). *Duhuran* is a verbal noun, because the meaning of *yuqdhafun* is *yudhharun* (they are repelled). One says *dahartuhu dahran wa duhuran*, meaning "I drove him away." As-Sulami and Ya'qub al-Hadrami read *duhuran* with a fatha on the *dal*, which is a verbal noun on the pattern *fu'ul*. As for al-Farra', he took it as an active participle (*ism al-fa'il*), meaning: "they are pelted with that which repels them," that is, with a repulsion (*duhur*), then the *ba'* was dropped. The parallels to this are: **"The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind"** [Ghafir: 57], and His saying: **"Are you stronger in creation, or the sky?"** [al-Nazi'at: 27].

**"We created them from clay that cleaves (lazib)"**, that is, sticky, said Ibn 'Abbas. From this is the saying of 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him):

*Learn, for Allah has increased you in stature... and all good characters are cleaving to you (lazib).*

Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: the meaning of *lazib* is *laziq* (adhering). Al-Mawardi said: The difference between *lasiq* (clinging) and *laziq* (adhering) is that *lasiq* is that which has stuck part to part, while *laziq* is that which sticks to whatever touches it. 'Ikrimah said: *lazib* means *lazij* (viscous). Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: that is, good and pure, which sticks to the hand. Mujahid said: *lazib* means *lazim* (necessary, lasting). The Arabs say *tin lazib* and *tin lazim*, substituting the *ba'* for the *mim*. Similar to this is their saying *latib* and *lazim*, with the *ba'* replacing the *mim*. *Al-lazib* means the firm, established; one says: "the thing became a *darbat lazib*," and this is more eloquent than *lazim*. Al-Nabighah said:

*And do not think that good has no evil after it, nor think that evil is a lasting blow (darbat lazib).*

Al-Farra' related from the Arabs: *tin latib*, meaning *lazim*. *Al-latib* means the firm; from it one says: *lataba yalTubu latban wa lutuban*, like *lazuba yazubu* with a *dammah*, *luzuban*. Abu al-Jarrah recited, concerning *al-latib*:

*If this is from date-wine that I drank, and I have departed from drinking date-wine, (I am) latā'ib (afflicted)*

*a headache, and the bones being broken, and a lethargy, and a nausea (ghamm) with the illumination within the belly, (it is) latib.* [Note: the wording of "ghamm" follows the narration in Lisan; the narration of al-Tabari has "ghathayan".]

*Al-latib* also means the adhering, like *al-lazib*; this was related from al-Asma'i and transmitted by al-Jawhari. Al-Suddi and al-Kalbi said concerning *al-lazib*: it is the pure (khalis). Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: it is the foul-smelling (muntin).

**"Nay, you are amazed, and they mock"**: the reading of the people of Madinah, Abu 'Amr and 'Asim is with a *fatha* on the *ta'*, addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, meaning: "Nay, you are amazed at what has been revealed to you of the Qur'an, while they mock it." This is also the reading of Shurayh, who rejected the reading with a *dammah* and said: "Allah is not amazed at anything; only one who does not know is amazed." It was also said: the meaning is "Nay, you are amazed at their denial of resurrection." The Kufans, except 'Asim, read it with a *dammah* on the *ta'*, and Abu 'Ubayd and al-Farra' preferred it; it is transmitted from 'Ali and Ibn Mas'ud. Shu'bah related from al-A'mash, from Abu Wa'il, from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud that he read: "Bal 'ajibtu" with a *dammah* on the *ta'*. It is also related from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Farra' said regarding His saying: "Nay, you are amazed, and they mock," the people read it with a *fatha* and with a *dammah* on the *ta'*, and the *dammah* is more beloved to me, because it is from 'Ali, 'Abd Allah and Ibn 'Abbas. Abu Zakariyya al-Farra' said: amazement, if it is attributed to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, its meaning is not from Allah as its meaning is from His servants; likewise His saying: "Allah mocks them" is not from Allah as its meaning is from the servants. In this is an explanation of the refutation of Shurayh's statement when he denied the reading with it. Jarir and al-A'mash related from Abu Wa'il Shaqiq ibn Salamah who said: "'Abd Allah (meaning Ibn Mas'ud) read it: 'Bal 'ajibtu wa yaskharun'." Shurayh said: "Allah is not amazed at anything; only one who does not know is amazed." Al-A'mash said: I mentioned this to Ibrahim, and he said: Shurayh was pleased with his own opinion; 'Abd Allah was more knowledgeable than Shurayh, and 'Abd Allah used to read it: "Bal 'ajibtu."

Al-Harawi said: Some of the imams said: the meaning of His saying "Bal 'ajibta" is: "Nay, I have requited them for their amazement," because Allah the Exalted related of them in more than one place their amazement at the truth, saying: **"And they were amazed that a warner from among themselves came to them"** [Sad: 4], and He said: "Indeed this is a strange thing (shay' ujab)," and **"Is it a wonder for mankind that We revealed to a man from among them?"** [Yunus: 2]. Then He said, "Nay, you are amazed," meaning: "Nay, I have requited them for the amazement." I say: this completes the meaning of al-Farra's statement, and al-Bayhaqi preferred it. Ali ibn Sulayman said: the meaning of both readings is one; the estimate is: "It was said, O Muhammad, 'Nay, you are amazed,'" because the Prophet ﷺ is addressed by the Qur'an. Al-Nahhas said: this is a good opinion, and omitting "it was said" (idmar al-qawl) is common. Al-Bayhaqi said: the first is more correct. Al-Mahdawi said: It is also possible that Allah's report about Himself of amazement is taken to mean that He manifested from His command and His wrath upon those who disbelieved in Him what stands in place of amazement among created beings, just as His report about Himself of laughing toward one He is pleased with, as came in the report from the Prophet ﷺ, is taken to mean that He manifested toward him from His pleasure what stands in place of laughter among created beings, figuratively and by extension. Al-Harawi said: It is said that the meaning of "your Lord is amazed" is "He is pleased and rewards," so He named it amazement though it is not amazement in reality, as Allah said: **"And Allah plans"** [al-Anfal: 30], meaning "Allah requites them for their plotting." Similar to this in the hadith is "Your Lord is amazed at your despair and your despairing." Amazement may also mean that the act is great in the sight of Allah. So the meaning of His saying "Nay, you are amazed" is: "Nay, their deed is great in My sight." Al-Bayhaqi said: This may be the meaning of the hadith of 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Your Lord is amazed at a young man who has no youthful folly." Likewise is what al-Bukhari recorded from Abu Hurayrah from the Prophet ﷺ who said: "Allah is amazed at a people who enter Paradise in chains." Al-Bayhaqi said: This hadith and what comes like it may mean that He amazes His angels with His generosity and compassion toward His servants, when He brings them to faith in Him through fighting and capture in chains, until when they believe He admits them into Paradise. It was also said: the meaning of "Nay, you are amazed" is "Nay, I denied." Related by al-Naqqash. Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: amazement from Allah is denial of a thing and its magnification, and this is the language of the Arabs. It has come in a report: "Your Lord is amazed at your despair and your despairing."

**"And they mock"**: it was said that the *waw* is the *waw* of circumstance: "I am amazed at them in the state of their mocking." It was also said: the sentence is complete at His saying "Nay, you are amazed," then He resumed: "and they mock," meaning: at what you brought when you recite it to them. It was also said: they mock you when you call them.

**"And when they are reminded"**: that is, when they are admonished with the Qur'an. According to Qatadah's view, "they do not remember" means they do not benefit from it. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: that is, when they are told what befell the deniers before them, they turn away from it and do not reflect.

**"And when they see a sign"**: that is, a miracle, **"they mock (yastaskhirun)"**: that is, they ridicule, according to Qatadah, and they say it is sorcery. *Istaskhara* and *sakhira* have the same meaning, like *istaqarra* and *qarra*, and *is'ajaba* and *'ajiba*. It was also said: "yastaskhirun" means they request mockery from others. Mujahid said: they ridicule. It was also said: they think that sign is mockery.

**"And they say: This is nothing but clear sorcery"**: that is, when they are unable to counter the miracles with anything, they say this is sorcery, imagination and deception.

**"When we die and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be raised?"** That is, will we be resurrected when we have died? It is an interrogative of denial and mockery on their part. **"Or our forefathers of old?"** That is, or will our forefathers be resurrected? The interrogative particle *alif* has entered upon the conjunctive particle. Nafi' read *"aw abaؤuna"* with a sukun on the *waw*. This was already discussed in Surat al-A'raf, in His saying: **"Or were the people of the cities secure?"** [al-A'raf: 98].

**Qur'an 37:18–21 in al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran)**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say: Yes﴾, meaning: yes, you will be raised up. "And you will be humbled (dakhirun)", meaning: abased and humiliated, because when they see the fulfilment of what they denied, they will inevitably be humbled. It is also said: the meaning is that the Resurrection will certainly take place despite your dislike, so this is a matter that will occur in spite of you, even though you deny it today according to your own claim.

"It will be but a single blast (zajrah wahidah)", meaning: a single cry. This is the view of al-Hasan, and it is the second blast (al-nafkhah al-thaniyah). The cry is called a zajrah because its purpose is to drive (zajr), that is, people are driven by it as camels and horses are driven when they are herded. "Then, behold, they will be standing", looking, "meaning: some of them will look at others." It is also said: the meaning is that they will await what will be done to them. It is also said: this is like His saying: ﴿Then, behold, the eyes of those who disbelieved will be fixed in horror﴾ (Al-Anbiya' 21:97). It is also said: meaning, they will look at the resurrection that they denied.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿They will say, "Woe to us! This is the Day of Judgment."﴾ They call down woe upon themselves, because on that Day they will know what has befallen them. The word (waylana) is in the accusative because it is a verbal noun (masdar) according to the Basran grammarians. Al-Farra' claimed that its underlying form is "ya wayla lana", with "wayl" meaning grief. Al-Nahhas said: If it were as he said, it would be written separately, but in the Mushaf it is written joined, and we know of no one who writes it except joined.

"The Day of Judgment (yawm al-din)" means the Day of Reckoning. It is also said: the Day of Recompense.

﴿This is the Day of Decision, which you used to deny﴾. It is said that this is the words of some of them to others, meaning: this is the Day we used to deny. It is also said that it is the words of Allah the Exalted to them. It is also said that it is the words of the angels, meaning: this is the Day of Judgment between people, when the righteous is distinguished from the falsifier. Then: ﴿a party in the Garden and a party in the Blaze﴾ (Al-Shura 42:7).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 37, verse 22–35:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Gather those who did wrong, and their spouses﴾. This is from the saying of God, exalted is He, to the angels: "Gather the polytheists and their spouses," that is, their companions in polytheism. Polytheism (shirk) is wrongdoing (zulm), as God, exalted is He, says: ﴿Indeed, associating others with God is a great wrong﴾ [Luqman: 13]. So the disbeliever is gathered with the disbeliever. This was said by Qatadah and Abu al-'Aliyah. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said, regarding the saying of God, mighty and majestic is He: "Gather those who did wrong and their spouses," he said: the adulterer with the adulterer, the wine-drinker with the wine-drinker, and the possessor of theft with the possessor of theft. Ibn 'Abbas said: "and their spouses" means their likes (ashbahahum). This goes back to the saying of 'Umar. It was also said: "and their spouses" means their wives who agreed with them in disbelief. This was said by Mujahid and al-Hasan, and al-Nu'man ibn Bashir related it from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. Al-Dahhak said: "and their spouses" means their companions among the devils. This is also the view of Muqatil: every disbeliever is gathered with his devil in a chain. "And what they used to worship besides God" — of the idols, the devils and Iblis. "Then guide them to the path of Hellfire": that is, drive them to the Fire. It was also said: "then guide them" means direct them. It is said: "I guided him to the road" and "I guided him the road," meaning I showed him it. And "I gave the gift (ahdaytu al-hadiyyah)" and "I guided the bride (hadaytu al-'arus)," and it is said "ahdaytuha," meaning I made her in the position of a gift.

His saying, exalted is He: "And stop them, for they are to be questioned." Isa ibn 'Umar related it as "annahum" with a fatha on the hamzah. Al-Kisa'i said: that is, "li-annahum" and "bi-annahum." It is said: "I stopped the beast (waqaftu al-dabbah) — aqifuha waqfan — and it stopped itself (fawaqafat hiya wuqufan)," it is transitive and intransitive, meaning: consider them. This occurs before driving them to Hellfire, and there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in it, meaning: stop them for reckoning, then drive them to the Fire. It was also said: they are driven to the Fire first, then they are gathered for questioning when they draw near the Fire. "Indeed they are to be questioned" about their deeds, their sayings and their actions. Al-Qurazi and al-Kalbi said, and al-Dahhak: about their sins. Ibn 'Abbas: about "There is no god but God." And also from him: about wronging the creation. In all of this is evidence that the disbeliever is held to account. This has already been discussed in "al-Hijr" [[See vol. 10, p. 60, first or second edition.]]. It was also said that their questioning is that it will be said to them: "Did there not come to you messengers from among you?" [al-An'am: 130], establishing the proof. And it will be said to them: "What is the matter with you that you do not help one another?" in the manner of rebuke and reproach, that is, one of you should help another and so prevent him from the punishment of God. It was also said: this alludes to the saying of Abu Jahl on the day of Badr: "We are a united company seeking victory" [al-Qamar: 44]. Its original form is "tatanasarun," and one of the two taa' was dropped for lightness. Al-Bazzi doubled the taa' in connection.

His saying, exalted is He: "Rather, they are today submitting (mustaslimun)." Qatadah said: submitting to the punishment of God, mighty and majestic is He. Ibn 'Abbas: humbled and abased. Al-Hasan: yielding. Al-Akhfash: casting down their hands. The meanings are close. "And some of them turn to others, questioning one another (yatasa'alun)" — meaning the leaders and the followers — "yatakhasamun" (disputing). It is said: "la yatasa'alun," so the "la" was dropped. Al-Nahhas said: the ignorant of the language erred, imagining that this is from His saying: ﴿So there will be no kinship between them that Day, nor will they ask one another﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 101]; rather it means they will not ask one another by kinship, so one of them says: "I ask you by the ties of kinship between me and you, that you benefit me, or that you drop a right you have over me, or that you grant me a good deed." This is clear, because before it is ﴿So there will be no kinship between them﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 101], meaning they will not benefit by the kinship ties between them, as came in the hadith: "A man is pleased to have a claim against his father or his son, and he takes it from him, for these are the good deeds and the evil deeds." And in another hadith: "May God have mercy on a man who had an injustice against his brother concerning wealth or honour, so he came to him and sought his forgiveness before he was called to account, for he would otherwise take from his good deeds, and if he had no good deeds, evil deeds of the one he wronged would be added to his own." "Yatasa'alun" here means that some of them ask others and rebuke them for having misled them or opened a door to disobedience. What demonstrates this is that after it comes: "Indeed you used to come to us from the right." Mujahid said: this is the saying of the disbelievers to the devils. Qatadah: it is the saying of mankind to the jinn. It was also said: it is from the saying of the followers to the leaders, evidenced by the saying of God, exalted is He: ﴿If you could see when the wrongdoers are made to stand before their Lord, returning words to one another﴾ [Saba': 31], etc. Sa'id related from Qatadah: that is, you come to us by way of good and turn us away from it. Something similar is related from Ibn 'Abbas. It was also said: you come to us from the "right" which we love and by which we take omens, so that you deceive us through it under the guise of counsel. The Arabs take omens from what comes from the right and call it "al-sanih." It was also said: "you come to us from the right" means you come to us as one who, if he swears to us, we believe him. It was also said: you come to us from the direction of religion, so you make the matter of the Law seem light to us and make us averse to it. I say: this view is very good, because good and evil come from the direction of religion, and "al-yamin" (the right) here carries the sense of religion, meaning you used to adorn error for us. It was also said: "al-yamin" means strength, meaning you restrain us by force, dominance and compulsion. God, exalted is He, says: ﴿Then he turned upon them, striking with the right hand﴾ [al-Saffat: 93], meaning with strength, and the strength of a man is in his right hand. The poet said:

Whenever a banner is raised for glory... and 'Arabah meets it with the right hand

meaning with strength and power. This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said: "you come to us from the right," meaning from the side of the truth, that it is with you; and all of these are close in meaning. "They will say: Rather, you were not believers." Qatadah said: this is the saying of the devils to them. It was also said: it is from the saying of the leaders, meaning: you were never believers until we moved you from it to disbelief; rather you were upon disbelief and remained upon it through habit and custom. "And we had no authority over you" — that is, no proof for abandoning the truth. "Rather, you were a transgressing people" — that is, astray, exceeding the limit. "So the word of our Lord has come into effect against us" — this too is from the saying of the followed, meaning: the word of our Lord has become binding upon us and upon you, so all of us will taste the punishment, as God wrote and informed through the tongues of the messengers: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men all together﴾ [al-Sajdah: 13]. This accords with the hadith: "God, mighty and majestic is He, wrote for the Fire its people and for Paradise its people, neither increased nor decreased among them." "So we misled you" — that is, we adorned for you what you were upon of disbelief, "for we ourselves were misguided" — through whispering and invitation. Then He said, informing about them: "Indeed, they on that Day are sharers in the punishment," the misguided and the misleader. "Indeed, that is how We deal with the criminals" — that is, like this act — meaning the polytheists. "Indeed, when it was said to them, 'There is no god but God,' they were arrogant" — that is, when it was said to them, "Say," the saying was omitted.

"They were arrogant" is in the accusative position as the predicate of "kanu" (was). It may also be in the nominative position as the predicate of "inna," with "kana" being inoperative. When the Prophet ﷺ said to Abu Talib at his death, with the Quraysh gathered: "Say, 'There is no god but God,' and by it you will rule the Arabs, and the non-Arabs will submit to you," they refused and were disdainful of that. Abu Hurayrah related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "God, exalted is He, revealed in His Book, mentioning a people who were arrogant, and said: ﴿Indeed, when it was said to them, 'There is no god but God,' they were arrogant﴾." And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿When those who disbelieved put into their hearts zealotry, the zealotry of the Jahiliyyah; then God sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers and made them adhere to the word of piety, and they were most deserving of it and worthy of it﴾ [al-Fath: 26]. This is from the saying of God, exalted is He, to the angels: "Gather the polytheists and their spouses," that is, their companions in polytheism. This was said by Qatadah and Abu al-'Aliyah. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said, regarding the saying of God, mighty and majestic is He: "Gather those who did wrong and their spouses," he said: the adulterer with the adulterer, the wine-drinker with the wine-drinker, and the possessor of theft with the possessor of theft. Ibn 'Abbas said: "and their spouses" means their likes (ashbahahum). This goes back to the saying of 'Umar. It was also said: "and their spouses" means their wives who agreed with them in disbelief. This was said by Mujahid and al-Hasan, and al-Nu'man ibn Bashir related it from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. Al-Dahhak said: "and their spouses" means their companions among the devils. This is also the view of Muqatil: every disbeliever is gathered with his devil in a chain. "And what they used to worship besides God" — of the idols, the devils and Iblis. "Then guide them to the path of Hellfire": that is, drive them to the Fire. It was also said: "then guide them" means direct them. It is said: "I guided him to the road" and "I guided him the road," meaning I showed him it. And "I gave the gift (ahdaytu al-hadiyyah)" and "I guided the bride (hadaytu al-'arus)," and it is said "ahdaytuha," meaning I made her in the position of a gift.

His saying, exalted is He: "And stop them, for they are to be questioned." Isa ibn 'Umar related it as "annahum" with a fatha on the hamzah. Al-Kisa'i said: that is, "li-annahum" and "bi-annahum." It is said: "I stopped the beast (waqaftu al-dabbah) — aqifuha waqfan — and it stopped itself (fawaqafat hiya wuqufan)," it is transitive and intransitive, meaning: consider them. This occurs before driving them to Hellfire, and there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in it, meaning: stop them for reckoning, then drive them to the Fire. It was also said: they are driven to the Fire first, then they are gathered for questioning when they draw near the Fire. "Indeed they are to be questioned" about their deeds, their sayings and their actions. Al-Qurazi and al-Kalbi said, and al-Dahhak: about their sins. Ibn 'Abbas: about "There is no god but God." And also from him: about wronging the creation. In all of this is evidence that the disbeliever is held to account. This has already been discussed in "al-Hijr" [[See vol. 10, p. 60, first or second edition.]]. It was also said that their questioning is that it will be said to them: "Did there not come to you messengers from among you?" [al-An'am: 130], establishing the proof. And it will be said to them: "What is the matter with you that you do not help one another?" in the manner of rebuke and reproach, that is, one of you should help another and so prevent him from the punishment of God. It was also said: this alludes to the saying of Abu Jahl on the day of Badr: "We are a united company seeking victory" [al-Qamar: 44]. Its original form is "tatanasarun," and one of the two taa' was dropped for lightness. Al-Bazzi doubled the taa' in connection.

His saying, exalted is He: "Rather, they are today submitting (mustaslimun)." Qatadah said: submitting to the punishment of God, mighty and majestic is He. Ibn 'Abbas: humbled and abased. Al-Hasan: yielding. Al-Akhfash: casting down their hands. The meanings are close. "And some of them turn to others, questioning one another (yatasa'alun)" — meaning the leaders and the followers — "yatakhasamun" (disputing). It is said: "la yatasa'alun," so the "la" was dropped. Al-Nahhas said: the ignorant of the language erred, imagining that this is from His saying: ﴿So there will be no kinship between them that Day, nor will they ask one another﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 101]; rather it means they will not ask one another by kinship, so one of them says: "I ask you by the ties of kinship between me and you, that you benefit me, or that you drop a right you have over me, or that you grant me a good deed." Something similar is related from Ibn 'Abbas. It was also said: you come to us from the "right" which we love and by which we take omens, so that you deceive us through it under the guise of counsel. The Arabs take omens from what comes from the right and call it "al-sanih." It was also said: "you come to us from the right" means you come to us as one who, if he swears to us, we believe him. It was also said: you come to us from the direction of religion, so you make the matter of the Law seem light to us and make us averse to it. I say: this view is very good, because good and evil come from the direction of religion, and "al-yamin" (the right) here carries the sense of religion, meaning you used to adorn error for us. It was also said: "al-yamin" means strength, meaning you restrain us by force, dominance and compulsion. God, exalted is He, says: ﴿Then he turned upon them, striking with the right hand﴾ [al-Saffat: 93], meaning with strength, and the strength of a man is in his right hand. The poet said:

Whenever a banner is raised for glory... and 'Arabah meets it with the right hand

meaning with strength and power. This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said: "you come to us from the right," meaning from the side of the truth, that it is with you; and all of these are close in meaning. "They will say: Rather, you were not believers." Qatadah said: this is the saying of the devils to them. It was also said: it is from the saying of the leaders, meaning: you were never believers until we moved you from it to disbelief; rather you were upon disbelief and remained upon it through habit and custom. "And we had no authority over you" — that is, no proof for abandoning the truth. "Rather, you were a transgressing people" — that is, astray, exceeding the limit. "So the word of our Lord has come into effect against us" — this too is from the saying of the followed, meaning: the word of our Lord has become binding upon us and upon you, so all of us will taste the punishment, as God wrote and informed through the tongues of the messengers: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men all together﴾ [al-Sajdah: 13]. This accords with the hadith: "God, mighty and majestic is He, wrote for the Fire its people and for Paradise its people, neither increased nor decreased among them." "So we misled you" — that is, we adorned for you what you were upon of disbelief, "for we ourselves were misguided" — through whispering and invitation. Then He said, informing about them: "Indeed, they on that Day are sharers in the punishment," the misguided and the misleader. "Indeed, that is how We deal with the criminals" — that is, like this act — meaning the polytheists. "Indeed, when it was said to them, 'There is no god but God,' they were arrogant" — that is, when it was said to them, "Say," the saying was omitted.

"They were arrogant" is in the accusative position as the predicate of "kanu" (was). It may also be in the nominative position as the predicate of "inna," with "kana" being inoperative. When the Prophet ﷺ said to Abu Talib at his death, with the Quraysh gathered: "Say, 'There is no god but God,' and by it you will rule the Arabs, and the non-Arabs will submit to you," they refused and were disdainful of that. Abu Hurayrah related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "God, exalted is He, revealed in His Book, mentioning a people who were arrogant, and said: ﴿Indeed, when it was said to them, 'There is no god but God,' they were arrogant﴾." And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿When those who disbelieved put into their hearts zealotry, the zealotry of the Jahiliyyah; then God sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers and made them adhere to the word of piety, and they were most deserving of it and worthy of it﴾ [al-Fath: 26]. That word is "There is no god but God, Muhammad is the Messenger of God," which the polytheists were arrogant toward on the day of Hudaybiyyah, the day the Messenger of God ﷺ made the agreement with them concerning the terms of the truce. Al-Bayhaqi related this report, and al-Qushayri related the one before it.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 37, verse 22–35:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Gather those who did wrong, and their spouses﴾. This is from the saying of God, exalted is He, to the angels: "Gather the polytheists and their spouses," that is, their companions in polytheism. Polytheism (shirk) is wrongdoing (zulm), as God, exalted is He, says: ﴿Indeed, associating others with God is a great wrong﴾ [Luqman: 13]. So the disbeliever is gathered with the disbeliever. This was said by Qatadah and Abu al-'Aliyah. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said, regarding the saying of God, mighty and majestic is He: "Gather those who did wrong and their spouses," he said: the adulterer with the adulterer, the wine-drinker with the wine-drinker, and the possessor of theft with the possessor of theft. Ibn 'Abbas said: "and their spouses" means their likes (ashbahahum). This goes back to the saying of 'Umar. It was also said: "and their spouses" means their wives who agreed with them in disbelief. This was said by Mujahid and al-Hasan, and al-Nu'man ibn Bashir related it from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. Al-Dahhak said: "and their spouses" means their companions among the devils. This is also the view of Muqatil: every disbeliever is gathered with his devil in a chain. "And what they used to worship besides God" — of the idols, the devils and Iblis. "Then guide them to the path of Hellfire": that is, drive them to the Fire. It was also said: "then guide them" means direct them. It is said: "I guided him to the road" and "I guided him the road," meaning I showed him it. And "I gave the gift (ahdaytu al-hadiyyah)" and "I guided the bride (hadaytu al-'arus)," and it is said "ahdaytuha," meaning I made her in the position of a gift.

His saying, exalted is He: "And stop them, for they are to be questioned." Isa ibn 'Umar related it as "annahum" with a fatha on the hamzah. Al-Kisa'i said: that is, "li-annahum" and "bi-annahum." It is said: "I stopped the beast (waqaftu al-dabbah) — aqifuha waqfan — and it stopped itself (fawaqafat hiya wuqufan)," it is transitive and intransitive, meaning: consider them. This occurs before driving them to Hellfire, and there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in it, meaning: stop them for reckoning, then drive them to the Fire. It was also said: they are driven to the Fire first, then they are gathered for questioning when they draw near the Fire. "Indeed they are to be questioned" about their deeds, their sayings and their actions. Al-Qurazi and al-Kalbi said, and al-Dahhak: about their sins. Ibn 'Abbas: about "There is no god but God." And also from him: about wronging the creation. In all of this is evidence that the disbeliever is held to account. This has already been discussed in "al-Hijr" [[See vol. 10, p. 60, first or second edition.]]. It was also said that their questioning is that it will be said to them: "Did there not come to you messengers from among you?" [al-An'am: 130], establishing the proof. And it will be said to them: "What is the matter with you that you do not help one another?" in the manner of rebuke and reproach, that is, one of you should help another and so prevent him from the punishment of God. It was also said: this alludes to the saying of Abu Jahl on the day of Badr: "We are a united company seeking victory" [al-Qamar: 44]. Its original form is "tatanasarun," and one of the two taa' was dropped for lightness. Al-Bazzi doubled the taa' in connection.

His saying, exalted is He: "Rather, they are today submitting (mustaslimun)." Qatadah said: submitting to the punishment of God, mighty and majestic is He. Ibn 'Abbas: humbled and abased. Al-Hasan: yielding. Al-Akhfash: casting down their hands. The meanings are close. "And some of them turn to others, questioning one another (yatasa'alun)" — meaning the leaders and the followers — "yatakhasamun" (disputing). It is said: "la yatasa'alun," so the "la" was dropped. Al-Nahhas said: the ignorant of the language erred, imagining that this is from His saying: ﴿So there will be no kinship between them that Day, nor will they ask one another﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 101]; rather it means they will not ask one another by kinship, so one of them says: "I ask you by the ties of kinship between me and you, that you benefit me, or that you drop a right you have over me, or that you grant me a good deed." This is clear, because before it is ﴿So there will be no kinship between them﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 101], meaning they will not benefit by the kinship ties between them, as came in the hadith: "A man is pleased to have a claim against his father or his son, and he takes it from him, for these are the good deeds and the evil deeds." And in another hadith: "May God have mercy on a man who had an injustice against his brother concerning wealth or honour, so he came to him and sought his forgiveness before he was called to account, for he would otherwise take from his good deeds, and if he had no good deeds, evil deeds of the one he wronged would be added to his own." "Yatasa'alun" here means that some of them ask others and rebuke them for having misled them or opened a door to disobedience. What demonstrates this is that after it comes: "Indeed you used to come to us from the right." Mujahid said: this is the saying of the disbelievers to the devils. Qatadah: it is the saying of mankind to the jinn. It was also said: it is from the saying of the followers to the leaders, evidenced by the saying of God, exalted is He: ﴿If you could see when the wrongdoers are made to stand before their Lord, returning words to one another﴾ [Saba': 31], etc. Sa'id related from Qatadah: that is, you come to us by way of good and turn us away from it. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 37, verse 36–40:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And they say, "Shall we really abandon our gods for a mad poet?"﴾ That is, for the saying of a mad poet. So Allah, mighty and majestic, responded to them, saying: "Nay, he has brought the truth," meaning the Qur'an and the Oneness of God (tawhid), "and he has confirmed the messengers," in what they brought of tawhid. "Indeed, you are going to taste the painful punishment." The original form is "la-dha'iqun" (lada'iqun), so the nun was dropped for lightness and the word was put in the genitive because of the idafa (annexation). It is also permissible to put it in the accusative, as Sibawayh recited:

"So I found him not seeking to please, nor remembering God except a little."

Sibawayh also permitted "wa-l-muqimi as-salat" (and those who establish prayer) on this basis. ﴿And you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do.﴾ That is, you will only be recompensed for what you did of polytheism. ﴿Except the chosen servants of Allah.﴾ This is an exception from those who taste the punishment. The reading of the people of Medina and Kufa is "al-mukhlaṣīn" with a fatha on the lam, meaning those whom Allah has purified for His obedience, His religion and His guardianship. The rest read it with a kasra on the lam, meaning those who sincerely devoted worship to Allah. It has also been said that this is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), meaning: "Indeed, you, O criminals, are tasters of the punishment, but the chosen servants of Allah do not taste the punishment."

**Verse 41–49 (al-Qurtubi, *al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an*)**

Allah's words: ﴿For them is a known provision﴾. He means the sincere servants (al-mukhlasin), that is, they have a known gift that does not cease. Qatadah said: it means Paradise. Others said: it means the provision of Paradise. It was also said: it refers to the fruits that were mentioned. Muqatil said: "whenever they desire it." Ibn al-Sa'ib said: it is according to the measure of morning and evening, as Allah says: ﴿And they will have their provision therein morning and evening﴾ [Maryam: 62]. "Fawakih" is the plural of "fakihah" (fruit). Allah says: ﴿And We increased them with fruit﴾ [al-Tur: 22], and it means all fruits, fresh and dried, as Ibn 'Abbas said. "In Gardens of Bliss" means that they also have honour from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, through the raising of ranks, hearing His speech, and meeting Him. "In Gardens of Bliss" means in orchards in which they enjoy delights. It has already been mentioned that the gardens are seven, in Surah Yunus [[See vol. 8, p. 329 and what follows, in its printed edition or its first edition.]], among them al-Na'im (the Garden of Bliss).

Allah's words: ﴿on couches facing one another﴾. 'Ikrimah and Mujahid said: they do not look at the back of one another, as a sign of closeness and mutual love. It was also said: the couches turn with them however they wish, so no one sees the back of another. Ibn 'Abbas said: on couches adorned with pearls, rubies and chrysolite (zabarjad). The "sarir" (couch) is as far as the distance between San'a' and al-Jabiyah, and between 'Adan and Ayla. It was also said: they turn with the people of a single dwelling. And Allah knows best.

Allah's words: ﴿They will be served with a cup from a flowing spring﴾. Having mentioned their food, He mentioned their drink. According to the lexicographers (ahl al-lughah), "al-ka's" (cup) is a term that includes every vessel together with its drink; if it is empty, it is not a ka's. Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: every "ka's" in the Qur'an means wine. The Arabs call a vessel a "ka's" when it contains wine, and when it contains no wine they call it "ina'" (vessel) and "qadah" (bowl). Al-Nahhas said: a trustworthy lexicographer related that the Arabs call a bowl containing wine "ka's," and when it has no wine it is a "qadah," just as a tablecloth (khiwan) with food on it is called "ma'idah" (table), but when there is no food on it you do not call it a ma'idah. Abu al-Hasan Ibn Kaysan said: from this comes "za'inah" for a litter (howdah) when a woman is in it. Al-Zajjaj said: "with a cup from a flowing spring" means from wine that flows as springs flow over the surface of the earth. "Al-Ma'in" is flowing, visible water. "Bayda'" (white) is an attribute of the cup, and it was also said that it is an attribute of the wine. "Ladhdhah lil-sharibin" (delicious to the drinkers). Al-Hasan said: the wine of Paradise is whiter than milk. Regarding "ladhdhah," al-Zajjaj said: that is, having delight, and the noun was omitted. It was also said: it is a verbal noun (masdar) made into an adjective, meaning delicious white wine, as one says "sharab ladhdh" and "ladhidh," like "nabat ghadd" and "ghadid." As for the saying of the poet [[It is al-Ra'i. It is also narrated:

"And delicious like the taste of Sarkhad wine, which I left behind
In the enemy's land, out of fear of misfortunes."

Sarkhad is a place to which a wine is attributed. He meant that when he entered the lands of his enemies he did not sleep, out of fear of them.]]:

"And delicious like the taste of Sarkhadi wine that I left
In the land of enemies, out of fear of misfortunes,"

it means sleep. It was also said: "bayda'" means that men have not pressed it with their feet. ﴿Neither will there be in it any intoxication﴾, that is, it does not overpower their minds, and no sickness or headache comes to them from it. ﴿Nor will they be drained by it﴾, that is, their minds do not depart through drinking it. It is said: "wine is a ghawl (a destroyer) of forbearance, and war is a ghawl of souls," meaning it takes them away. And it is said: "nuzifa al-rajul yunzaf, fahuwa manzuf and nazif" when he becomes drunk. Imru' al-Qays said:

"And when she walks, like the walk of the drunk one, whom
Exhaustion and breathlessness throw down at the sand-dune."

[[Al-Bahr: exhaustion and loss of breath.]]

He also said:

"A drunk one, when she stands up to walk, sways,
And she shields her heart, the tender one, lest it be intoxicated."

[[Al-Khatr: a weakness that takes hold of one after drinking medicine or poison. He says she is drunk from wine; when she stands up to walk she feels languor and sluggishness in her bones, so she conceals her heart and shields it lest it make her suffer in her walking.]]

Another said [[He is Jamil ibn Ma'mar. It is also said the verse is by 'Umar ibn Abi Rabi'ah. "Al-Hashraj" is a hollow in the mountain where water gathers and becomes clear.]]:

"So I kissed her mouth, taking hold of her horns,
And the drunk one drank the cool water of al-Hashraj."

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited it with a kasrah on the zay, from "anzafa al-qawm," when the time of "nazf" (drunkenness) came upon them. It is said: "ahsada al-zar' " when its harvest time came, "aqtafa al-karm" when its gathering time came, and "arkaba al-muhr" when its riding time came. It was also said: the meaning is that they do not exhaust their drink, because that is their habit. It is said: "anzafa al-rajul fahuwa manzuf" when his wine has run out. Al-Hutay'ah said [[Attributed to al-Jawhari, al-Yalab, and al-Abyardi. Abjar is Abjar ibn Jabir al-'Ijli, and he was a Christian.]]:

"By my life, if you have run out of wine or become sober,
Then wretched were the drinking companions, you, the family of Abjar."

Al-Nahhas said: the first recitation is clearer and more correct in meaning, because the meaning of "yunzafun" according to the leading exegetes, among them Mujahid, is that their minds do not depart. Allah's words: ﴿And with them will be those restraining their gaze﴾, that is, women who have restricted their gaze to their husbands so that they look at no others. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and others. 'Ikrimah: "qasirat al-tarf" means confined to their husbands. The first interpretation is clearer, because the verse does not say "maqsurat" (confined), but another verse says "maqsurat," whose explanation will come. "Qasirat" is derived from their saying: "qad iqtasara 'ala kadha" when he is content with it and turns away from others. Imru' al-Qays said:

"Of the restraining-gazed ones, if a small ant were to crawl
Over a white garment of theirs, it would leave a mark."

It is also narrated: "on the cheek." The first is more eloquent. "Al-Itb" is a garment, and "al-Mahwal" is a small ant. Mujahid also said: its meaning is that they do not seduce. "'In" is plural of "'aynah," meaning large-eyed; al-Suddi said so. Mujahid: "'in" means beautiful eyes. Al-Hasan: those whose whites are very white and whose blacks are very black. The first is more common in the language. It is said: "rajul a'yan," wide-eyed, clear-eyed, and the plural is "'in." Its root is "fu'l" with a damma, and the 'ayn was given a kasrah so that the waw would not become ya'. From this, wild cattle are called "'in," the bull is "a'yan," and the cow is "'ayna'." ﴿As if they were preserved eggs﴾, that is, guarded. Al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd said: they are compared to ostrich eggs, which the ostrich covers with feathers against wind and dust, so their colour is white with a yellowish tinge, which is the finest colour of women. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi said: they are compared to the inner part of an egg before it is peeled and touched by hands. 'Ata' said: they are compared to the membrane that lies between the outer shell and the yolk of the egg. "Saha'" of anything is its skin, and the plural is "sahan," as al-Jawhari said. Similar is the saying of al-Tabari: it is the thin skin that lies on the egg between these two. A similar report is also narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ). The Arabs liken a woman to an egg for its clarity and whiteness. Imru' al-Qays said:

"And an egg of a veiled tent, whose pavilion is not approached,
And I enjoyed with her a pleasure not hastened."

When the Arabs describe a thing as beautiful and clean, they say: "as if it were an ostrich egg covered with feathers." It was also said: "maknun" means guarded against breakage, that is, they are virgins. It was also said: "al-bid" refers to pearls, as in His words: ﴿And maidens with wide eyes, like preserved pearls﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 22–23], that is, in their shells, as Ibn 'Abbas also said. From this is the saying of the poet:

"She is white like a pearl of the deep sea,
Separated from a hidden jewel."

He said "maknun" while "bid" is plural, because he returned the adjective to the wording (lafz).

**Verse 41–49 (al-Qurtubi, *al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an*)**

Allah's words: ﴿For them is a known provision﴾. He means the sincere servants (al-mukhlasin), that is, they have a known gift that does not cease. Qatadah said: it means Paradise. Others said: it means the provision of Paradise. It was also said: it refers to the fruits that were mentioned. Muqatil said: "whenever they desire it." Ibn al-Sa'ib said: it is according to the measure of morning and evening, as Allah says: ﴿And they will have their provision therein morning and evening﴾ [Maryam: 62]. "Fawakih" is the plural of "fakihah" (fruit). Allah says: ﴿And We increased them with fruit﴾ [al-Tur: 22], and it means all fruits, fresh and dried, as Ibn 'Abbas said. "In Gardens of Bliss" means that they also have honour from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, through the raising of ranks, hearing His speech, and meeting Him. "In Gardens of Bliss" means in orchards in which they enjoy delights. It has already been mentioned that the gardens are seven, in Surah Yunus [[See vol. 8, p. 329 and what follows, in its printed edition or its first edition.]], among them al-Na'im (the Garden of Bliss).

Allah's words: ﴿on couches facing one another﴾. 'Ikrimah and Mujahid said: they do not look at the back of one another, as a sign of closeness and mutual love. It was also said: the couches turn with them however they wish, so no one sees the back of another. Ibn 'Abbas said: on couches adorned with pearls, rubies and chrysolite (zabarjad). The "sarir" (couch) is as far as the distance between San'a' and al-Jabiyah, and between 'Adan and Ayla. It was also said: they turn with the people of a single dwelling. And Allah knows best.

Allah's words: ﴿They will be served with a cup from a flowing spring﴾. Having mentioned their food, He mentioned their drink. According to the lexicographers (ahl al-lughah), "al-ka's" (cup) is a term that includes every vessel together with its drink; if it is empty, it is not a ka's. Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: every "ka's" in the Qur'an means wine. The Arabs call a vessel a "ka's" when it contains wine, and when it contains no wine they call it "ina'" (vessel) and "qadah" (bowl). Al-Nahhas said: a trustworthy lexicographer related that the Arabs call a bowl containing wine "ka's," and when it has no wine it is a "qadah," just as a tablecloth (khiwan) with food on it is called "ma'idah" (table), but when there is no food on it you do not call it a ma'idah. Abu al-Hasan Ibn Kaysan said: from this comes "za'inah" for a litter (howdah) when a woman is in it. Al-Zajjaj said: "with a cup from a flowing spring" means from wine that flows as springs flow over the surface of the earth. "Al-Ma'in" is flowing, visible water. "Bayda'" (white) is an attribute of the cup, and it was also said that it is an attribute of the wine. "Ladhdhah lil-sharibin" (delicious to the drinkers). Al-Hasan said: the wine of Paradise is whiter than milk. Regarding "ladhdhah," al-Zajjaj said: that is, having delight, and the noun was omitted. It was also said: it is a verbal noun (masdar) made into an adjective, meaning delicious white wine, as one says "sharab ladhdh" and "ladhidh," like "nabat ghadd" and "ghadid." As for the saying of the poet [[It is al-Ra'i. It is also narrated:

"And delicious like the taste of Sarkhad wine, which I left behind
In the enemy's land, out of fear of misfortunes."

Sarkhad is a place to which a wine is attributed. He meant that when he entered the lands of his enemies he did not sleep, out of fear of them.]]:

"And delicious like the taste of Sarkhadi wine that I left
In the land of enemies, out of fear of misfortunes,"

it means sleep. It was also said: "bayda'" means that men have not pressed it with their feet. ﴿Neither will there be in it any intoxication﴾, that is, it does not overpower their minds, and no sickness or headache comes to them from it. ﴿Nor will they be drained by it﴾, that is, their minds do not depart through drinking it. It is said: "wine is a ghawl (a destroyer) of forbearance, and war is a ghawl of souls," meaning it takes them away. And it is said: "nuzifa al-rajul yunzaf, fahuwa manzuf and nazif" when he becomes drunk. Imru' al-Qays said:

"And when she walks, like the walk of the drunk one, whom
Exhaustion and breathlessness throw down at the sand-dune."

[[Al-Bahr: exhaustion and loss of breath.]]

He also said:

"A drunk one, when she stands up to walk, sways,
And she shields her heart, the tender one, lest it be intoxicated."

[[Al-Khatr: a weakness that takes hold of one after drinking medicine or poison. He says she is drunk from wine; when she stands up to walk she feels languor and sluggishness in her bones, so she conceals her heart and shields it lest it make her suffer in her walking.]]

Another said [[He is Jamil ibn Ma'mar. It is also said the verse is by 'Umar ibn Abi Rabi'ah. "Al-Hashraj" is a hollow in the mountain where water gathers and becomes clear.]]:

"So I kissed her mouth, taking hold of her horns,
And the drunk one drank the cool water of al-Hashraj."

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited it with a kasrah on the zay, from "anzafa al-qawm," when the time of "nazf" (drunkenness) came upon them. It is said: "ahsada al-zar' " when its harvest time came, "aqtafa al-karm" when its gathering time came, and "arkaba al-muhr" when its riding time came. It was also said: the meaning is that they do not exhaust their drink, because that is their habit. It is said: "anzafa al-rajul fahuwa manzuf" when his wine has run out. Al-Hutay'ah said [[Attributed to al-Jawhari, al-Yalab, and al-Abyardi. Abjar is Abjar ibn Jabir al-'Ijli, and he was a Christian.]]:

"By my life, if you have run out of wine or become sober,
Then wretched were the drinking companions, you, the family of Abjar."

Al-Nahhas said: the first recitation is clearer and more correct in meaning, because the meaning of "yunzafun" according to the leading exegetes, among them Mujahid, is that their minds do not depart. Thus Allah, Mighty and Majestic, negated from the wine of Paradise the afflictions that befall the wine of this world, such as headache and intoxication. The correct meaning of "yunzafun," as it is said, is: "anzafa al-rajul" when his drink ran out, but this is unlikely to be used of the drink of Paradise; its figurative sense would be that it never runs out. It was also said: "la yunzifun" with a kasrah on the zay means they do not become intoxicated; this was mentioned by al-Zajjaj and Abu 'Ali, as mentioned by al-Qushayri. Al-Mahdawi said: its meaning cannot be that they become intoxicated, because before it is "la fiha ghawl," that is, their minds are not destroyed, and so it would be a repetition, although repetition is acceptable in al-Waqi'ah. It is possible that the meaning of "la fiha ghawl" is that they do not fall ill, so the meaning of "wa la hum 'anha yunzafun" would be that they do not become intoxicated, or that their drink does not run out. Qatadah said: "al-ghawl" is stomach pain. Likewise Ibn Abi Najih narrated from Mujahid: "la fiha ghawl," he said: there is no stomach pain in it. Al-Hasan said: headache. This is also the saying of Ibn 'Abbas: "la fiha ghawl," there is no headache in it. Al-Dahhak related from him that he said: wine has four qualities: intoxication, headache, vomiting and urination, so Allah mentioned the wine of Paradise and cleared it of these qualities. Mujahid said: disease. Ibn Kaysan said: colic. These sayings are close in meaning. Al-Kalbi said: "la fiha ghawl" means sin, and its counterpart is: ﴿No idle talk therein, nor sinfulness﴾ [al-Tur: 23]. Al-Sha'bi, al-Suddi and Abu 'Ubaydah said: they do not destroy their minds so as to take them away. From this is the saying of the poet:

"The cup kept destroying us,
And taking away the first, one by one."

That is, it strikes down one after another. Allah removed intoxication from the people of Paradise only so that their enjoyment of their bliss would not be cut off. The people of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: "al-ghawl" is corruption that occurs in secret. It is said: "ightalahu ightiyalan" when he spoiled his affair for him in secret. From it come "al-ghawl" and "al-ghilah," which is killing in secret.

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 37, verses 50–61:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then some of them will turn to others, questioning one another.﴾ That is, they will converse among themselves about their worldly affairs. This is part of the completeness of intimacy in Paradise. It is coordinated with the meaning of "they are served with" (yutaf 'alayhim, "a cup is passed around to them"), so the meaning is that they drink and converse over the wine, as drinkers customarily do. One of them said:

"Nothing remains of pleasures except... the talk of the noble over the wine."

So one of them will turn to another, asking about what happened to them and what happened against them in the world. However, it is expressed in the past tense, in keeping with God's way in His reports.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿A speaker among them will say﴾, that is, one of the people of Paradise: "Indeed, I had a companion" (qarin), that is, a close constant friend, "who used to say: 'Are you truly among those who affirm?'" That is, affirm the Resurrection and the recompense. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "His qarin is his partner." Their two stories and the disagreement over their names were already covered in al-Kahf, at His saying, Exalted is He: "And present to them a parable of two men" [[See vol. 10, p. 399 and following, of this edition, first or second printing.]]. About the two of them God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: "A speaker among them will say, 'Indeed, I had a companion,'" down to "among those brought forth [to the Fire]." It was also said that by the qarin he meant his companion from the devils, who used to whisper to him the denial of the Resurrection.

It was read as "a'innaka la-mina al-musaddiqin" (with a shaddah on the sad), transmitted by Ali ibn Kaysah from Sulaym from Hamzah. Al-Nahhas said: "It is not permissible to read 'a'innaka la-mina al-musaddiqin' with a shaddah, because the word has no meaning here in the sense of charity (tasaddaq)." Al-Qushayri said: "In a reading transmitted from Hamzah: 'a'innaka la-mina al-musaddiqin' with a shaddah on the sad." It was objected that this is from taṣdiq (affirmation), not from tasaddu (giving charity). The objection is baseless, because when a recitation (qira'ah, a canonical variant reading) is established from the Prophet ﷺ, there is no room for criticizing it. So the meaning is: "Are you among those who give charity (with wealth), seeking reward in the Hereafter?" ﴿When we die and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be recompensed?﴾ That is, shall we be repaid and called to account after death?

Then God, Exalted is He, says to the people of Paradise: ﴿Would you look down?﴾ It was also said that this is the saying of the believer to his brothers in Paradise: "Would you look down toward the Fire, so we may see what has become of that companion?" It was also said that it is the saying of the angels. "Would you look down" is not an interrogative; rather it has the sense of a command, "Look down!" This was said by Ibn al-A'rabi and others. From the same usage: when the verse on wine was revealed, Umar stood before the Prophet ﷺ, then raised his head to the sky and said: "O Lord, make a clearer explanation about wine that would satisfy us." Then the verse was revealed: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 91]. He said: Umar then called out, "We have desisted, O our Lord."

Ibn Abbas read "hal antum muṭli'un" (with the ta' sukun and light), and "fa-uṭli'a" (with a hamzat al-qat' and light). The meaning is "Will you come forward?" and so he came forward. Al-Nahhas said: "'Fa-uṭli'a fa-ra'ah' has two interpretations: first, that it is a future verb, meaning 'so I shall look down,' and it is in the subjunctive as the answer to the interrogative. Second, that it is a past verb, and uṭli'a and aṭṭala'a are one and the same." Al-Zajjaj said: "It is said ṭala'a, aṭla'a, and iṭṭala'a with one meaning." It has also been reported as "hal antum muṭṭali'ūna" with a kasrah on the nun, but Abu Hatim and others rejected this. Al-Nahhas said: "This is not permissible, because it combines the nun with the idafah (annexation), and if it were annexed it would be 'hal antum muṭli'iyya.'" Although Sibawayh and al-Farra' both transmitted something like it and cited:

"They are the ones who say the good and command it, / and when they fear a great matter from a sudden event..."

Al-Farra' also cited: "wa-l-fa'iluna-hu" (and the doers of it). Sibawayh alone cited:

"He did not lean, while the people were gathered for him, all of them, and the hands of the ones who reproach were surrounding him."

[[Its completion: "jamī'an wa-aydī al-mu'ni'īna rawāhiquh." He means: the ones who reproach surrounded him, and they are the ones who ask; the people gathered for the gift, so he sat before them in a state of humble, unassuming sitting, not leaning.]]

This is an anomaly outside the usage of the Arabs, and such a thing is not to be cited in the Book of God, nor is it counted as eloquent Arabic. It has been suggested in explanation that he treated the active participle as if it were the present tense, because of their closeness, so muṭṭali'ūn is treated like yaṭla'ūn. This was mentioned by Abu al-Fath Uthman ibn Jinni, who cited:

"Have you seen, if I bring him a youth and a boy / and he wears striped garments..."

"Aqā'ilunna aḥḍirū al-shuhūdā" (Will you say, "Bring the witnesses!"?)

He treated "a-qā'ilunna" as if it were "a-taqūlūna" (will you say). [[Another version reads "aḥḍirī," addressed to a woman, which is the proper reading according to what al-Radi cited in Khizanat al-Adab, where he said: al-'Ayni transmitted "aḥḍirū" with a waw for the plural, but there is no basis for it. The verse was cited by al-Sukkari in Ash'ar Hudhayl from a man of theirs with the wording: "Aqā'ilūna a'jilu al-shuhūdā."]]

Ibn Abbas, regarding God's saying: ﴿Would you look down? Then he looked down and saw him﴾, said: "In Paradise there are openings through which its people look down on the Fire and its people." Ka'b said the same, as transmitted by Ibn al-Mubarak. He said: "Between Paradise and the Fire there are openings. When a believer wants to look at an enemy he had in the world, he looks down through one of the openings." God, Exalted is He, says: ﴿Then he looked down and saw him in the midst of the Blazing Fire.﴾

That is, in the middle of the Fire, with the thorny plant (ḥasak) all around him. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud. It is said: "I was exhausted until my sawā' (middle) was cut off," that is, my midst. From Abu Ubaydah: Isa ibn Umar said to me, "I used to write, O Abu Ubaydah, until my sawā' was cut off." From Qatadah, he said: Some scholars said: "Had God, Mighty and Majestic, not made him recognize him, he would not have recognized him, for his appearance (ḥabr) and form (sabr) had changed." [[al-ḥabr wa-l-sabr: color and appearance.]]

At that point he says: ﴿By God, you almost brought me to ruin!﴾ Here "in" is the lightened form of the heavy particle, which entered upon kad as it enters upon kana. Similar is ﴿Indeed, he almost led us astray﴾ [al-Furqan: 42]. The lam is the one that distinguishes it from the negative particle. ﴿And were it not for the favor of my Lord, I would have been among those brought forth.﴾ That is, into the Fire.

Al-Kisa'i said: "Latardīnī" means "to destroy me," and al-radā is destruction. Al-Mubarrad said: "If it were said 'latardīnī' (to cast me into destruction), 'to bring me into the Fire,' it would be permissible." ﴿And were it not for the favor of my Lord﴾, that is, His protection and His guidance in holding to the handhold of Islam and disavowing the evil companion. What follows "law-la" (were it not for) is in the nominative by the mubtada' (inceptive) according to Sibawayh, and the predicate is omitted. ﴿I would have been among those brought forth.﴾ Al-Farra' said: "That is, I would have been with you in the Fire, brought forth." And "aḥḍara" (to bring forth) is used absolutely only for evil, as al-Mawardi said.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then is it not that we shall not die﴾ — it was read as "bi-māʾitīn" (with the hamzah). The hamzah in "afa-mā" is the interrogative, entering upon the fa' of conjunction, and the conjoined element is omitted. Its meaning is: "Are we to be eternal and blessed, and so we shall not die nor be punished?" ﴿Except our first death﴾ — this is an exception that is not of the first part, and it is a verbal noun (maṣdar), because it is qualified. This is from the saying of the people of Paradise to the angels, when death is slaughtered. It is said: "O people of Paradise, eternity and no death; O people of the Fire, eternity and no death."

It was also said: it is from the saying of the believer by way of recounting God's blessing, in that they will not die nor be punished, meaning: this is our state and our description. It was also said: it is from the saying of the believer as a rebuke to the disbeliever, because of his denial of the Resurrection, and that there is nothing but death in the world. Then the believer said, pointing to what he was in: ﴿Indeed, this is the great triumph.﴾ "Huwa" may be the subject (mubtada'), and what follows is the predicate concerning it, and the whole clause is the predicate of inna. It is also permissible for "huwa" to be a separating pronoun (fasl).

﴿For the like of this let the workers work.﴾ It may be from the saying of the believer when he saw what God had prepared for him in Paradise and what He had given him: he said, "For the like of this" bounty and grace, "let the workers work." This is the counterpart of what the disbeliever said to him: ﴿I am greater than you in wealth and mightier in men﴾ [al-Kahf: 34]. It may also be from the saying of the angels. It was also said: it is from the saying of God, Mighty and Majestic, to the people of the world, meaning: you have heard what is in Paradise of good things and reward, and "for the like of this" reward, "let the workers work." Al-Nahhas said: The sense of the sentence, and God knows best, is: "Let the workers work for the like of this." If someone says: the fa' in Arabic indicates that the second comes after the first, so how can what follows it be intended as preceding? The answer is that the preceding is like the following, because the rule for the prepositions and what follows them is that they be placed later.
