The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 37, verses 50–61:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then some of them will turn to others, questioning one another.﴾ That is, they will converse among themselves about their worldly affairs. This is part of the completeness of intimacy in Paradise. It is coordinated with the meaning of "they are served with" (yutaf 'alayhim, "a cup is passed around to them"), so the meaning is that they drink and converse over the wine, as drinkers customarily do. One of them said:

"Nothing remains of pleasures except... the talk of the noble over the wine."

So one of them will turn to another, asking about what happened to them and what happened against them in the world. However, it is expressed in the past tense, in keeping with God's way in His reports.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿A speaker among them will say﴾, that is, one of the people of Paradise: "Indeed, I had a companion" (qarin), that is, a close constant friend, "who used to say: 'Are you truly among those who affirm?'" That is, affirm the Resurrection and the recompense. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "His qarin is his partner." Their two stories and the disagreement over their names were already covered in al-Kahf, at His saying, Exalted is He: "And present to them a parable of two men" [[See vol. 10, p. 399 and following, of this edition, first or second printing.]]. About the two of them God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: "A speaker among them will say, 'Indeed, I had a companion,'" down to "among those brought forth [to the Fire]." It was also said that by the qarin he meant his companion from the devils, who used to whisper to him the denial of the Resurrection.

It was read as "a'innaka la-mina al-musaddiqin" (with a shaddah on the sad), transmitted by Ali ibn Kaysah from Sulaym from Hamzah. Al-Nahhas said: "It is not permissible to read 'a'innaka la-mina al-musaddiqin' with a shaddah, because the word has no meaning here in the sense of charity (tasaddaq)." Al-Qushayri said: "In a reading transmitted from Hamzah: 'a'innaka la-mina al-musaddiqin' with a shaddah on the sad." It was objected that this is from taṣdiq (affirmation), not from tasaddu (giving charity). The objection is baseless, because when a recitation (qira'ah, a canonical variant reading) is established from the Prophet ﷺ, there is no room for criticizing it. So the meaning is: "Are you among those who give charity (with wealth), seeking reward in the Hereafter?" ﴿When we die and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be recompensed?﴾ That is, shall we be repaid and called to account after death?

Then God, Exalted is He, says to the people of Paradise: ﴿Would you look down?﴾ It was also said that this is the saying of the believer to his brothers in Paradise: "Would you look down toward the Fire, so we may see what has become of that companion?" It was also said that it is the saying of the angels. "Would you look down" is not an interrogative; rather it has the sense of a command, "Look down!" This was said by Ibn al-A'rabi and others. From the same usage: when the verse on wine was revealed, Umar stood before the Prophet ﷺ, then raised his head to the sky and said: "O Lord, make a clearer explanation about wine that would satisfy us." Then the verse was revealed: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 91]. He said: Umar then called out, "We have desisted, O our Lord."

Ibn Abbas read "hal antum muṭli'un" (with the ta' sukun and light), and "fa-uṭli'a" (with a hamzat al-qat' and light). The meaning is "Will you come forward?" and so he came forward. Al-Nahhas said: "'Fa-uṭli'a fa-ra'ah' has two interpretations: first, that it is a future verb, meaning 'so I shall look down,' and it is in the subjunctive as the answer to the interrogative. Second, that it is a past verb, and uṭli'a and aṭṭala'a are one and the same." Al-Zajjaj said: "It is said ṭala'a, aṭla'a, and iṭṭala'a with one meaning." It has also been reported as "hal antum muṭṭali'ūna" with a kasrah on the nun, but Abu Hatim and others rejected this. Al-Nahhas said: "This is not permissible, because it combines the nun with the idafah (annexation), and if it were annexed it would be 'hal antum muṭli'iyya.'" Although Sibawayh and al-Farra' both transmitted something like it and cited:

"They are the ones who say the good and command it, / and when they fear a great matter from a sudden event..."

Al-Farra' also cited: "wa-l-fa'iluna-hu" (and the doers of it). Sibawayh alone cited:

"He did not lean, while the people were gathered for him, all of them, and the hands of the ones who reproach were surrounding him."

[[Its completion: "jamī'an wa-aydī al-mu'ni'īna rawāhiquh." He means: the ones who reproach surrounded him, and they are the ones who ask; the people gathered for the gift, so he sat before them in a state of humble, unassuming sitting, not leaning.]]

This is an anomaly outside the usage of the Arabs, and such a thing is not to be cited in the Book of God, nor is it counted as eloquent Arabic. It has been suggested in explanation that he treated the active participle as if it were the present tense, because of their closeness, so muṭṭali'ūn is treated like yaṭla'ūn. This was mentioned by Abu al-Fath Uthman ibn Jinni, who cited:

"Have you seen, if I bring him a youth and a boy / and he wears striped garments..."

"Aqā'ilunna aḥḍirū al-shuhūdā" (Will you say, "Bring the witnesses!"?)

He treated "a-qā'ilunna" as if it were "a-taqūlūna" (will you say). [[Another version reads "aḥḍirī," addressed to a woman, which is the proper reading according to what al-Radi cited in Khizanat al-Adab, where he said: al-'Ayni transmitted "aḥḍirū" with a waw for the plural, but there is no basis for it. The verse was cited by al-Sukkari in Ash'ar Hudhayl from a man of theirs with the wording: "Aqā'ilūna a'jilu al-shuhūdā."]]

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 37, verses 50–61:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then some of them will turn to others, questioning one another.﴾ That is, they will converse among themselves about their worldly affairs. This is part of the completeness of intimacy in Paradise. It is coordinated with the meaning of "they are served with" (yutaf 'alayhim, "a cup is passed around to them"), so the meaning is that they drink and converse over the wine, as drinkers customarily do. One of them said:

"Nothing remains of pleasures except... the talk of the noble over the wine."

So one of them will turn to another, asking about what happened to them and what happened against them in the world. However, it is expressed in the past tense, in keeping with God's way in His reports.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿A speaker among them will say﴾, that is, one of the people of Paradise: "Indeed, I had a companion" (qarin), that is, a close constant friend, "who used to say: 'Are you truly among those who affirm?'" That is, affirm the Resurrection and the recompense. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "His qarin is his partner." Their two stories and the disagreement over their names were already covered in al-Kahf, at His saying, Exalted is He: "And present to them a parable of two men" [[See vol. 10, p. 399 and following, of this edition, first or second printing.]]. About the two of them God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: "A speaker among them will say, 'Indeed, I had a companion,'" down to "among those brought forth [to the Fire]." It was also said that by the qarin he meant his companion from the devils, who used to whisper to him the denial of the Resurrection.

It was read as "a'innaka la-mina al-musaddiqin" (with a shaddah on the sad), transmitted by Ali ibn Kaysah from Sulaym from Hamzah. Al-Nahhas said: "It is not permissible to read 'a'innaka la-mina al-musaddiqin' with a shaddah, because the word has no meaning here in the sense of charity (tasaddaq)." So the meaning is: "Are you among those who give charity (with wealth), seeking reward in the Hereafter?" ﴿When we die and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be recompensed?﴾ That is, shall we be repaid and called to account after death?

Then God, Exalted is He, says to the people of Paradise: ﴿Would you look down?﴾ It was also said that this is the saying of the believer to his brothers in Paradise: "Would you look down toward the Fire, so we may see what has become of that companion?" Their two stories and the disagreement over their names were already covered in al-Kahf, at His saying, Exalted is He: "And present to them a parable of two men" [[See vol. 10, p. 399 and following, of this edition, first or second printing.]]. About the two of them God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: "A speaker among them will say, 'Indeed, I had a companion,'" down to "among those brought forth [to the Fire]." It was also said that by the qarin he meant his companion from the devils, who used to whisper to him the denial of the Resurrection.

It was read as "a'innaka la-mina al-musaddiqin" (with a shaddah on the sad), transmitted by Ali ibn Kaysah from Sulaym from Hamzah. Al-Nahhas said: "It is not permissible to read 'a'innaka la-mina al-musaddiqin' with a shaddah, because the word has no meaning here in the sense of charity (tasaddaq)." Al-Qushayri said: "In a reading transmitted from Hamzah: 'a'innaka la-mina al-musaddiqin' with a shaddah on the sad." It was objected that this is from taṣdiq (affirmation), not from tasaddu (giving charity). The objection is baseless, because when a recitation (qira'ah, a canonical variant reading) is established from the Prophet ﷺ, there is no room for criticizing it. So the meaning is: "Are you among those who give charity (with wealth), seeking reward in the Hereafter?" ﴿When we die and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be recompensed?﴾ That is, shall we be repaid and called to account after death?

Then God, Exalted is He, says to the people of Paradise: ﴿Would you look down?﴾ It was also said that this is the saying of the believer to his brothers in Paradise: "Would you look down toward the Fire, so we may see what has become of that companion?" It was also said that it is the saying of the angels. "Would you look down" is not an interrogative; rather it has the sense of a command, "Look down!" This was said by Ibn al-A'rabi and others. From the same usage: when the verse on wine was revealed, Umar stood before the Prophet ﷺ, then raised his head to the sky and said: "O Lord, make a clearer explanation about wine that would satisfy us." Then the verse was revealed: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 91]. He said: Umar then called out, "We have desisted, O our Lord."

Ibn Abbas read "hal antum muṭli'un" (with the ta' sukun and light), and "fa-uṭli'a" (with a hamzat al-qat' and light). The meaning is "Will you come forward?" and so he came forward. Al-Nahhas said: "'Fa-uṭli'a fa-ra'ah' has two interpretations: first, that it is a future verb, meaning 'so I shall look down,' and it is in the subjunctive as the answer to the interrogative. Second, that it is a past verb, and uṭli'a and aṭṭala'a are one and the same." Al-Zajjaj said: "It is said ṭala'a, aṭla'a, and iṭṭala'a with one meaning." It has also been reported as "hal antum muṭṭali'ūna" with a kasrah on the nun, but Abu Hatim and others rejected this. Al-Nahhas said: "This is not permissible, because it combines the nun with the idafah (annexation), and if it were annexed it would be 'hal antum muṭli'iyya.'" Although Sibawayh and al-Farra' both transmitted something like it and cited:

"They are the ones who say the good and command it, / and when they fear a great matter from a sudden event..."

Al-Farra' also cited: "wa-l-fa'iluna-hu" (and the doers of it). Sibawayh alone cited:

"He did not lean, while the people were gathered for him, all of them, and the hands of the ones who reproach were surrounding him."

[[Its completion: "jamī'an wa-aydī al-mu'ni'īna rawāhiquh." He means: the ones who reproach surrounded him, and they are the ones who ask; the people gathered for the gift, so he sat before them in a state of humble, unassuming sitting, not leaning.]]

This is an anomaly outside the usage of the Arabs, and such a thing is not to be cited in the Book of God, nor is it counted as eloquent Arabic. It has been suggested in explanation that he treated the active participle as if it were the present tense, because of their closeness, so muṭṭali'ūn is treated like yaṭla'ūn. This was mentioned by Abu al-Fath Uthman ibn Jinni, who cited:

"Have you seen, if I bring him a youth and a boy / and he wears striped garments..."

"Aqā'ilunna aḥḍirū al-shuhūdā" (Will you say, "Bring the witnesses!"?)

He treated "a-qā'ilunna" as if it were "a-taqūlūna" (will you say). [[Another version reads "aḥḍirī," addressed to a woman, which is the proper reading according to what al-Radi cited in Khizanat al-Adab, where he said: al-'Ayni transmitted "aḥḍirū" with a waw for the plural, but there is no basis for it. The verse was cited by al-Sukkari in Ash'ar Hudhayl from a man of theirs with the wording: "Aqā'ilūna a'jilu al-shuhūdā."]]

Ibn Abbas, regarding God's saying: ﴿Would you look down? Then he looked down and saw him﴾, said: "In Paradise there are openings through which its people look down on the Fire and its people." Ka'b said the same, as transmitted by Ibn al-Mubarak. He said: "Between Paradise and the Fire there are openings. When a believer wants to look at an enemy he had in the world, he looks down through one of the openings." God, Exalted is He, says: ﴿Then he looked down and saw him in the midst of the Blazing Fire.﴾

That is, in the middle of the Fire, with the thorny plant (ḥasak) all around him. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud. It is said: "I was exhausted until my sawā' (middle) was cut off," that is, my midst. From Abu Ubaydah: Isa ibn Umar said to me, "I used to write, O Abu Ubaydah, until my sawā' was cut off." From Qatadah, he said: Some scholars said: "Had God, Mighty and Majestic, not made him recognize him, he would not have recognized him, for his appearance (ḥabr) and form (sabr) had changed." [[al-ḥabr wa-l-sabr: color and appearance.]]

At that point he says: ﴿By God, you almost brought me to ruin!﴾ Here "in" is the lightened form of the heavy particle, which entered upon kad as it enters upon kana. Similar is ﴿Indeed, he almost led us astray﴾ [al-Furqan: 42]. The lam is the one that distinguishes it from the negative particle. ﴿And were it not for the favor of my Lord, I would have been among those brought forth.﴾ That is, into the Fire.

Al-Kisa'i said: "Latardīnī" means "to destroy me," and al-radā is destruction. Al-Mubarrad said: "If it were said 'latardīnī' (to cast me into destruction), 'to bring me into the Fire,' it would be permissible." ﴿And were it not for the favor of my Lord﴾, that is, His protection and His guidance in holding to the handhold of Islam and disavowing the evil companion. And "aḥḍara" (to bring forth) is used absolutely only for evil, as al-Mawardi said.

Its meaning is: "Are we to be eternal and blessed, and so we shall not die nor be punished?" ﴿Except our first death﴾ — this is an exception that is not of the first part, and it is a verbal noun (maṣdar), because it is qualified. This is from the saying of the people of Paradise to the angels, when death is slaughtered. It is said: "O people of Paradise, eternity and no death; O people of the Fire, eternity and no death."

It was also said: it is from the saying of the believer by way of recounting God's blessing, in that they will not die nor be punished, meaning: this is our state and our description. It was also said: it is from the saying of the believer as a rebuke to the disbeliever, because of his denial of the Resurrection, and that there is nothing but death in the world. Then the believer said, pointing to what he was in: ﴿Indeed, this is the great triumph.﴾ "Huwa" may be the subject (mubtada'), and what follows is the predicate concerning it, and the whole clause is the predicate of inna. It is also permissible for "huwa" to be a separating pronoun (fasl).

﴿For the like of this let the workers work.﴾ It may be from the saying of the believer when he saw what God had prepared for him in Paradise and what He had given him: he said, "For the like of this" bounty and grace, "let the workers work." This is the counterpart of what the disbeliever said to him: ﴿I am greater than you in wealth and mightier in men﴾ [al-Kahf: 34]. It may also be from the saying of the angels. It was also said: it is from the saying of God, Mighty and Majestic, to the people of the world, meaning: you have heard what is in Paradise of good things and reward, and "for the like of this" reward, "let the workers work." Al-Nahhas said: The sense of the sentence, and God knows best, is: "Let the workers work for the like of this." If someone says: the fa' in Arabic indicates that the second comes after the first, so how can what follows it be intended as preceding? The answer is that the preceding is like the following, because the rule for the prepositions and what follows them is that they be placed later.

From Abu Ubaydah: Isa ibn Umar said to me, "I used to write, O Abu Ubaydah, until my sawā' was cut off." From Qatadah, he said: Some scholars said: "Had God, Mighty and Majestic, not made him recognize him, he would not have recognized him, for his appearance (ḥabr) and form (sabr) had changed." [[al-ḥabr wa-l-sabr: color and appearance.]]

At that point he says: ﴿By God, you almost brought me to ruin!﴾ Here "in" is the lightened form of the heavy particle, which entered upon kad as it enters upon kana. Similar is ﴿Indeed, he almost led us astray﴾ [al-Furqan: 42]. The lam is the one that distinguishes it from the negative particle. ﴿And were it not for the favor of my Lord, I would have been among those brought forth.﴾ That is, into the Fire.

Al-Kisa'i said: "Latardīnī" means "to destroy me," and al-radā is destruction. Al-Mubarrad said: "If it were said 'latardīnī' (to cast me into destruction), 'to bring me into the Fire,' it would be permissible." ﴿And were it not for the favor of my Lord﴾, that is, His protection and His guidance in holding to the handhold of Islam and disavowing the evil companion. What follows "law-la" (were it not for) is in the nominative by the mubtada' (inceptive) according to Sibawayh, and the predicate is omitted. ﴿I would have been among those brought forth.﴾ Al-Farra' said: "That is, I would have been with you in the Fire, brought forth." And "aḥḍara" (to bring forth) is used absolutely only for evil, as al-Mawardi said.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then is it not that we shall not die﴾ — it was read as "bi-māʾitīn" (with the hamzah). The hamzah in "afa-mā" is the interrogative, entering upon the fa' of conjunction, and the conjoined element is omitted. Its meaning is: "Are we to be eternal and blessed, and so we shall not die nor be punished?" ﴿Except our first death﴾ — this is an exception that is not of the first part, and it is a verbal noun (maṣdar), because it is qualified. This is from the saying of the people of Paradise to the angels, when death is slaughtered. It is said: "O people of Paradise, eternity and no death; O people of the Fire, eternity and no death."

It was also said: it is from the saying of the believer by way of recounting God's blessing, in that they will not die nor be punished, meaning: this is our state and our description. It was also said: it is from the saying of the believer as a rebuke to the disbeliever, because of his denial of the Resurrection, and that there is nothing but death in the world. Then the believer said, pointing to what he was in: ﴿Indeed, this is the great triumph.﴾ "Huwa" may be the subject (mubtada'), and what follows is the predicate concerning it, and the whole clause is the predicate of inna. It is also permissible for "huwa" to be a separating pronoun (fasl).

﴿For the like of this let the workers work.﴾ It may be from the saying of the believer when he saw what God had prepared for him in Paradise and what He had given him: he said, "For the like of this" bounty and grace, "let the workers work." This is the counterpart of what the disbeliever said to him: ﴿I am greater than you in wealth and mightier in men﴾ [al-Kahf: 34]. It may also be from the saying of the angels. It was also said: it is from the saying of God, Mighty and Majestic, to the people of the world, meaning: you have heard what is in Paradise of good things and reward, and "for the like of this" reward, "let the workers work." Al-Nahhas said: The sense of the sentence, and God knows best, is: "Let the workers work for the like of this." If someone says: the fa' in Arabic indicates that the second comes after the first, so how can what follows it be intended as preceding? The answer is that the preceding is like the following, because the rule for the prepositions and what follows them is that they be placed later.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 37, verse 62–68:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Is that better as a welcome (nuzul)?﴾ "That" is a mubtada' (subject) and "better" is a khabar (predicate), and it is from the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. "Nuzulan" is an specification (tamyiz). The meaning is: Is the delight of Paradise better as a welcome, or is the tree of zaqqum better as a welcome? The nuzul, linguistically, is provision that is abundant (al-Nahhas). Likewise nuzl, except that nuzl may be pronounced with the zay sukun in the language, and its origin may be nuzul; from it comes "uqimu lil-qawmi nuzulahum" (I prepare for the people their nuzul). Its derivation is that it is the food with which they can settle down and stay. This has already passed at the end of Surah Al 'Imran [[See vol. 4, p. 321, first or second edition.]] The tree of zaqqum is derived from al-tazaqqum, which is swallowing with difficulty because of its repulsiveness and stench. The exegetes said: It is in the sixth level, and it lives by the flame of fire just as a tree lives by cool water. So the people of the Fire must descend to it from above and eat from it, and likewise those below ascend to it. It has been disputed whether it is among the trees of this world that the Arabs know or not, on two opinions. One: it is known among the trees of this world. Those who held this view also differed about it. Qutrub said: It is a bitter tree that grows in Tihama, among the most wretched of trees. Others said: Rather, it is every deadly plant. The second opinion: It is not known among the trees of this world. When this verse about the tree of zaqqum was revealed, the disbelievers of Quraysh said: We do not know this tree. Then a man from Ifriqiya came to them and they asked him, and he said: With us it is butter and dates. Ibn al-Zib'ara said: May Allah increase zaqqum in our houses. Abu Jahl said to his slave-girl: "Tazaqqamina" (feed us zaqqum), so she brought him butter and dates. Then he said to his companions: "Tazaqqamu" (eat zaqqum). This is what Muhammad threatens us with; he claims that the Fire makes trees grow, and the Fire burns trees.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have made it a trial for the wrongdoers.﴾ That is, the polytheists. This is because they said: How can there be a tree in the Fire when it burns trees? This meaning has already passed in Surah Subhan [[See vol. 1, p. 283, first or second edition.]]. Their mockery in this is like their saying regarding His saying: ﴿Over it are nineteen﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 30]: What specifies this number? Until one of them said: "I will suffice you against them, so suffice me the rest." Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We have not made their number but a trial for those who disbelieved﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31]. Fitnah means testing. This statement of theirs was ignorance, for it is not impossible by reason that Allah creates in the Fire a tree of its own kind that the fire does not consume, just as Allah creates in it shackles, fetters, serpents, scorpions, and the guardians of the Fire. It was said: This disbelief that befell the disbelievers is what has now befallen the heretics, to the point that they interpret Paradise and Hellfire as pleasures or punishments that are spiritual, and they interpret the weighing of deeds, the Bridge, the Preserved Tablet and the Pen as meanings they have fabricated in themselves, apart from what the Muslims understood from the sources of the Shariah. When the report of the Truthful One comes concerning something that is imaginable to reason, it is obligatory to affirm it, even if it may be possible that it has an interpretation. Then, interpretation in a matter on which the Muslims agree is invalid interpretation that is not permitted, and the Muslims are unanimous on accepting these things without recourse to knowledge of the inner meaning. It was also said that it is a trial, that is, a punishment for the wrongdoers, as He said: ﴿Taste your trial; this is what you used to seek to hasten﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 14].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, it is a tree that emerges from the root of Hellfire.﴾ That is, the bottom of the Fire, and from it is its origin; then it branches out in Jahannam. "Its spathes (talh)": that is, its fruit, and it was named talh because it emerges (yatlu'). "As if its heads were the heads of devils." It was said: It means the devils themselves; He likened it to their heads because of their ugliness. The heads of devils are imagined in souls, even if they are not seen. From this is their saying for every ugly thing that it is like the form of a devil, and for every beautiful form that it is like the form of an angel. From this is the saying of Allah, the Exalted, reporting about the women of Yusuf: ﴿This is not a human; this is only a noble angel﴾ [Yusuf: 31]. This is an imaginative comparison, and its meaning was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Qurazi. From it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"And sharpened blue (arrows) like the fangs of ghouls" [[He meant by the sharpened blue ones arrows with sharp, clear points. The beginning of the verse:

"Will he kill me while the elevated (couches) are my resting places"]]. Although the ghoul is not known, yet this is because of what is imagined of its ugliness in souls. Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿Devils of mankind and jinn﴾ [al-An'am: 112], so the rebellious among mankind are visible devils. In the authentic hadith: "As if its palm-trees were the heads of devils." Many Arabs claimed to have seen devils and ghouls. Al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' said: The shayatin are serpents that have heads and crests, and they are among the most ugly and wretched of serpents and the lightest in body. A rajaz poet, comparing a woman to a serpent with a crest, said:

"Ghanjarad, who swears when I swear, and like the devil of al-Himat, the one with the crest"

The singular is himatah, and "al-a'raf" is the one that has a crest. Another poet describing his she-camel said:

"She plays with a Hadrami bridle-rein as if it were ... and a devil twists with a barren khurw-bush"

Ta'ammuj means crookedness in the course; a "sahm 'amuj" is an arrow that writhes in its flight; and "ta'ammajat al-hayyah" means the serpent wriggled as it moved. Another poet, describing the rein of the she-camel [[Thus in the original; perhaps the phrase and the verse here repeat what came before, and the correct wording of the first phrase is "a poet describing the rein of his riding-beast," adding the word "rein".]]:

"She plays with a Hadrami bridle-rein as if it were ... and a devil twists with a barren khurw-bush"

It was also said: That was likened only to a repulsive plant in Yemen called al-Astan and al-Shaytan. al-Nahhas said: This is not known among the Arabs. Al-Zamakhshari: It is a rough, stinking, bitter tree of hideous form whose fruit is called the heads of devils. al-Nahhas: It was also said: the shayatin are a kind of hideous serpent.

His saying: ﴿Then indeed they will eat from it and fill their bellies with it.﴾ So this is their food and fruit in place of the provision of the people of Paradise. He said in "al-Ghashiyah": ﴿There is for them no food except from dari'﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 6], and it will come. ﴿Then indeed for them upon it﴾ — that is, after eating from the tree — ﴿is a mixture of boiling water.﴾ Shawb means mixing; "shabb" and "shawb" are two dialects, like "faqr" and "fuqr," and the fatha is more famous. al-Farra' said: "shaba ta'amahu wa sharabahu" means when he mixed the two with something that mixes them, "shawban" and "shiyabah." So He informed that it is mixed for them. And hamim is hot water, to make it more horrible. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And they are given boiling water which cuts their intestines﴾ [Muhammad: 15]. al-Suddi said: The hamim is mixed for them with the pus of their eyes, the filth of their wounds, and their blood. It was also said: The zaqqum is mixed for them with the hamim, so that the bitterness of the zaqqum and the heat of the hamim are combined for them, as an intensification of their punishment and a renewal of their torment. ﴿Then indeed their return is to Hellfire.﴾ It was said: This indicates that when they ate the zaqqum they were in a punishment other than the Fire, and then they are returned to it. Muqatil said: The hamim is outside Jahim, so they are brought to the hamim to drink it, then they are returned to Jahim, due to the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿This is Jahannam which the criminals denied. They will circulate between it and boiling hot water﴾ [ar-Rahman: 43-44]. Ibn Mas'ud recited: "Then indeed their return is to Hellfire" (thumma inna munqalabahum la-ila al-jahim). Abu 'Ubaydah said: "thumma" may be used in the sense of "wa" (and). al-Qushayri: Perhaps the hamim is in a place of Jahannam on its edge.

It was also said: The zaqqum is mixed for them with the hamim, so that the bitterness of the zaqqum and the heat of the hamim are combined for them, as an intensification of their punishment and a renewal of their torment. ﴿Then indeed their return is to Hellfire.﴾ It was said: This indicates that when they ate the zaqqum they were in a punishment other than the Fire, and then they are returned to it. Muqatil said: The hamim is outside Jahim, so they are brought to the hamim to drink it, then they are returned to Jahim, due to the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿This is Jahannam which the criminals denied. They will circulate between it and boiling hot water﴾ [ar-Rahman: 43-44]. Ibn Mas'ud recited: "Then indeed their return is to Hellfire" (thumma inna munqalabahum la-ila al-jahim). Abu 'Ubaydah said: "thumma" may be used in the sense of "wa" (and). al-Qushayri: Perhaps the hamim is in a place of Jahannam on its edge.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 37, verse 62–68:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Is that better as a welcome (nuzul)?﴾ "That" is a mubtada' (subject) and "better" is a khabar (predicate), and it is from the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. "Nuzulan" is an specification (tamyiz). The meaning is: Is the delight of Paradise better as a welcome, or is the tree of zaqqum better as a welcome? The nuzul, linguistically, is provision that is abundant (al-Nahhas). Likewise nuzl, except that nuzl may be pronounced with the zay sukun in the language, and its origin may be nuzul; from it comes "uqimu lil-qawmi nuzulahum" (I prepare for the people their nuzul). Its derivation is that it is the food with which they can settle down and stay. This has already passed at the end of Surah Al 'Imran [[See vol. 4, p. 321, first or second edition.]] The tree of zaqqum is derived from al-tazaqqum, which is swallowing with difficulty because of its repulsiveness and stench. The exegetes said: It is in the sixth level, and it lives by the flame of fire just as a tree lives by cool water. So the people of the Fire must descend to it from above and eat from it, and likewise those below ascend to it. It has been disputed whether it is among the trees of this world that the Arabs know or not, on two opinions. One: it is known among the trees of this world. Those who held this view also differed about it. Qutrub said: It is a bitter tree that grows in Tihama, among the most wretched of trees. Others said: Rather, it is every deadly plant. The second opinion: It is not known among the trees of this world. When this verse about the tree of zaqqum was revealed, the disbelievers of Quraysh said: We do not know this tree. Then a man from Ifriqiya came to them and they asked him, and he said: With us it is butter and dates. Ibn al-Zib'ara said: May Allah increase zaqqum in our houses. Abu Jahl said to his slave-girl: "Tazaqqamina" (feed us zaqqum), so she brought him butter and dates. Then he said to his companions: "Tazaqqamu" (eat zaqqum). This is what Muhammad threatens us with; he claims that the Fire makes trees grow, and the Fire burns trees.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have made it a trial for the wrongdoers.﴾ That is, the polytheists. This is because they said: How can there be a tree in the Fire when it burns trees? This meaning has already passed in Surah Subhan [[See vol. 1, p. 283, first or second edition.]]. Their mockery in this is like their saying regarding His saying: ﴿Over it are nineteen﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 30]: What specifies this number? Until one of them said: "I will suffice you against them, so suffice me the rest." Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We have not made their number but a trial for those who disbelieved﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31]. Fitnah means testing. This statement of theirs was ignorance, for it is not impossible by reason that Allah creates in the Fire a tree of its own kind that the fire does not consume, just as Allah creates in it shackles, fetters, serpents, scorpions, and the guardians of the Fire. It was said: This disbelief that befell the disbelievers is what has now befallen the heretics, to the point that they interpret Paradise and Hellfire as pleasures or punishments that are spiritual, and they interpret the weighing of deeds, the Bridge, the Preserved Tablet and the Pen as meanings they have fabricated in themselves, apart from what the Muslims understood from the sources of the Shariah. When the report of the Truthful One comes concerning something that is imaginable to reason, it is obligatory to affirm it, even if it may be possible that it has an interpretation. Then, interpretation in a matter on which the Muslims agree is invalid interpretation that is not permitted, and the Muslims are unanimous on accepting these things without recourse to knowledge of the inner meaning. It was also said that it is a trial, that is, a punishment for the wrongdoers, as He said: ﴿Taste your trial; this is what you used to seek to hasten﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 14].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, it is a tree that emerges from the root of Hellfire.﴾ That is, the bottom of the Fire, and from it is its origin; then it branches out in Jahannam. "Its spathes (talh)": that is, its fruit, and it was named talh because it emerges (yatlu'). "As if its heads were the heads of devils." It was said: It means the devils themselves; He likened it to their heads because of their ugliness. The heads of devils are imagined in souls, even if they are not seen. From this is their saying for every ugly thing that it is like the form of a devil, and for every beautiful form that it is like the form of an angel. From this is the saying of Allah, the Exalted, reporting about the women of Yusuf: ﴿This is not a human; this is only a noble angel﴾ [Yusuf: 31]. This is an imaginative comparison, and its meaning was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Qurazi. From it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"And sharpened blue (arrows) like the fangs of ghouls" [[He meant by the sharpened blue ones arrows with sharp, clear points. The beginning of the verse:

"Will he kill me while the elevated (couches) are my resting places"]]. Although the ghoul is not known, yet this is because of what is imagined of its ugliness in souls. Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿Devils of mankind and jinn﴾ [al-An'am: 112], so the rebellious among mankind are visible devils. In the authentic hadith: "As if its palm-trees were the heads of devils." Many Arabs claimed to have seen devils and ghouls. Al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' said: The shayatin are serpents that have heads and crests, and they are among the most ugly and wretched of serpents and the lightest in body. A rajaz poet, comparing a woman to a serpent with a crest, said:

"Ghanjarad, who swears when I swear, and like the devil of al-Himat, the one with the crest"

The singular is himatah, and "al-a'raf" is the one that has a crest. Another poet describing his she-camel said:

"She plays with a Hadrami bridle-rein as if it were ... and a devil twists with a barren khurw-bush"

Ta'ammuj means crookedness in the course; a "sahm 'amuj" is an arrow that writhes in its flight; and "ta'ammajat al-hayyah" means the serpent wriggled as it moved. Another poet, describing the rein of the she-camel [[Thus in the original; perhaps the phrase and the verse here repeat what came before, and the correct wording of the first phrase is "a poet describing the rein of his riding-beast," adding the word "rein".]]:

"She plays with a Hadrami bridle-rein as if it were ... and a devil twists with a barren khurw-bush"

It was also said: That was likened only to a repulsive plant in Yemen called al-Astan and al-Shaytan. al-Nahhas said: This is not known among the Arabs. Al-Zamakhshari: It is a rough, stinking, bitter tree of hideous form whose fruit is called the heads of devils. al-Nahhas: It was also said: the shayatin are a kind of hideous serpent.

His saying: ﴿Then indeed they will eat from it and fill their bellies with it.﴾ So this is their food and fruit in place of the provision of the people of Paradise. He said in "al-Ghashiyah": ﴿There is for them no food except from dari'﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 6], and it will come. ﴿Then indeed for them upon it﴾ — that is, after eating from the tree — ﴿is a mixture of boiling water.﴾ Shawb means mixing; "shabb" and "shawb" are two dialects, like "faqr" and "fuqr," and the fatha is more famous. al-Farra' said: "shaba ta'amahu wa sharabahu" means when he mixed the two with something that mixes them, "shawban" and "shiyabah." So He informed that it is mixed for them. And hamim is hot water, to make it more horrible. It is said that the meaning of His words, "Indeed they found their fathers astray," is that they found them in that state and so followed them. "So they are hastening in their footsteps" means they are hurrying, related from Qatadah. Mujahid said: "like the manner of running at a trot." Al-Farra' said: "al-ihraa' (al-ihra') is hurrying with trembling." Abu 'Ubaydah said: "yuhra'un" means they urge on those behind them. The saying of al-Mubarrad is similar to this. He said: "al-muhri' is one who is urged on; it is said: 'So-and-so came hastening (yuhra'u) to the fire' when the cold urged him toward it." It is also said: they are driven by the intensity of their haste. Al-Fadl [said]... al-Zajjaj said: it is said "hura'a" and "uhri'a" when one is urged and driven.

His words, "And indeed most of the earlier peoples went astray before them," means most of the past nations. "And We certainly sent among them warners," meaning messengers who warned them of the punishment, but they disbelieved. "Then see how was the end of those who were warned," meaning the final outcome of their affair. "Except the chosen servants of Allah," meaning those whom Allah selected from disbelief. This has already been mentioned [[see vol. 1, p. 28, first or second edition.]]. Then it is said: this is an exception from "the warned." It is also said that it is from His words, "And indeed most of the earlier peoples went astray before them."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 37, verse 75–82:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Noah had certainly called Us﴾. The "nida'" (calling) here is in the sense of "istighatha" (seeking aid). It was said that he called upon Him by asking for the destruction of his people, and so he said: ﴿My Lord, leave not upon the earth from among the disbelievers a single dweller﴾ [Nuh: 26]. "So We were the best of responders." Al-Kisa'i said: meaning, "So We were the best of responders to him." "And We saved him and his family" – meaning the people of his religion, and they were those who believed with him, and they were eighty, as has preceded [see vol. 9, p. 35 of the first or second edition]. "From the great distress" – which is the drowning. "And We made his descendants the remaining ones." Ibn 'Abbas said: When Noah came out of the ship, everyone with him, men and women, died except his sons and his wives, and that is His saying: "And We made his descendants the remaining ones." Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: Noah had three sons, and all people are from the descendants of Noah: Sam, the father of the Arabs, Persia, the Romans, the Jews and the Christians; Ham, the father of the Sudanese, from the East to the West: the Sind, the Hind, the Nubians, the Zanj, the Abyssinians, the Copts, the Berbers and others; and Yafith, the father of the Slavs, the Turks, the Lan [and the Khazars], Ya'juj and Ma'juj, and what is beyond them.

Some people said: Others besides the sons of Noah also had offspring, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿the offspring of those whom We carried with Noah﴾ [al-Isra': 3], and His saying: ﴿It was said: O Noah, descend with peace from Us and blessings upon you and upon nations from those with you; and there will be nations We will grant enjoyment, then a painful punishment from Us will touch them﴾ [Hud: 48]. Accordingly, the meaning of the verse "And We made his descendants the remaining ones" is, to the exclusion of the descendants of those who disbelieved, whom We drowned.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We left for him among the later generations﴾, meaning: We left for him a good commendation in every nation, for he is beloved to all of them, to the extent that among the Magians there are those who say that he is Afridun. This meaning was related from Mujahid and others. Al-Kisa'i claimed that there are two interpretations of it: one of them is "And We left upon him among the later generations," as one says, "Peace be upon Noah," meaning: We left upon him this good commendation. This is the view of Abu al-'Abbas al-Mubarrad, meaning: We left upon him this word remaining, that is, they greet him with peace and pray for him, and this is from the reported speech, like His saying: ﴿A surah which We have sent down﴾ [al-Nur: 1]. The other view is that the meaning is "and We preserved upon him," and the speech is complete, then it begins: "Peace be upon Noah," meaning: safety for him from being mentioned with evil "among the later generations." Al-Kisa'i said: In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, "salaman" is in the accusative governed by "taraknا," meaning: We left upon him a good commendation, peace. It was also said: "among the later generations" means among the nation of Muhammad ﷺ. It was also said: among the prophets, since no prophet was sent after him except that he was commanded to follow him; God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿He has prescribed for you of religion that which He enjoined upon Noah﴾ [al-Shura: 13]. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: It has reached me that whoever, when he names [a child], says "Peace be upon Noah among the worlds," a scorpion will not sting him. Abu 'Umar mentioned it in al-Tamhid. In the Muwatta' from Khawla bint Hakim that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Whoever alights at a place, let him say: I seek refuge in the perfect words of God from the evil of what He has created, for nothing will harm him until he departs." And in it, from Abu Hurayra, that a man from Aslam said: "I did not sleep this night." The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "From what?" He said: "A scorpion stung me." The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Indeed, if you had said when you reached the evening: I seek refuge in the perfect words of God from the evil of what He created, it would not have harmed you."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good﴾, meaning: We preserve for them the good commendation. The kaf (ka) is in the position of the accusative, meaning: a reward such as this. "Indeed, he was among Our believing servants" – this is an explanation of his excellence.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then We drowned the others﴾, meaning: those who disbelieved. Its plural is "ukhar." The original form of it is that "min" should accompany it, but it was omitted, because the meaning is known, and "akhar" is not used except when something of its kind precedes it. "Thumma" here is not for sequence in time, but for enumerating blessings, like His saying: ﴿or a needy man in misery. Then he was among those who believed﴾ [al-Balad: 16–17], meaning: then I inform you that I drowned the others, namely those who lagged behind in faith.

It was also said: "among the later generations" means among the nation of Muhammad ﷺ. It was also said: among the prophets, since no prophet was sent after him except that he was commanded to follow him; God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿He has prescribed for you of religion that which He enjoined upon Noah﴾ [al-Shura: 13]. And in it, from Abu Hurayra, that a man from Aslam said: "I did not sleep this night." The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "From what?" He said: "A scorpion stung me." The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Indeed, if you had said when you reached the evening: I seek refuge in the perfect words of God from the evil of what He created, it would not have harmed you."

The original form of it is that "min" should accompany it, but it was omitted, because the meaning is known, and "akhar" is not used except when something of its kind precedes it. "Thumma" here is not for sequence in time, but for enumerating blessings, like His saying: ﴿or a needy man in misery. **The Qur'anic phrase: ﴿Is it a falsehood, gods other than Allah that you desire?﴾**

**The Qur'anic phrase: ﴿Then he glanced at the stars, and said, "Indeed, I am sick."﴾**

Ibn Zayd reported from his father: their king sent to him, "Tomorrow is our festival, so come out with us." He looked at a rising star and said, "Indeed, this rises along with my sickness." The science of the stars was in use among them and was studied, so he gave them the impression that he meant it in that sense. He showed them an excuse from their own belief for himself. They were people of herding and farming, and these two livelihoods require looking at the stars.

Juwaybir related from al-Dahhak: the science of the stars remained until the time of Jesus (peace be upon him). **The Qur'anic phrase: ﴿when he said to his father﴾**, who was Azar. The discussion of this has already passed. [[See vol. 7, p. 22, first or second edition.]]

**The Qur'anic phrase: ﴿and his people, "What is it that you worship?"﴾**

*Ma* may be in the nominative position as the subject, with *dha* as its predicate. It is also permissible for *ma* and *dha* to be in the accusative position, governed by *ta'budun* (you worship).

**The Qur'anic phrase: ﴿Is it a falsehood, gods other than Allah that you desire?﴾**

*Ifkan* is in the accusative as an object, in the sense of "Do you desire a falsehood?" Al-Mubarrad said: *al-ifk* is the worst kind of lying, which does not stand firm and is unstable; from it comes *ift'kafat bihim al-ard* (the earth overturned them).

*Alihatan* (gods) is a substitute (*badal*) for *ifkan*. ﴿other than Allah you desire﴾ means you worship. It is also permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause (*hal*), in the sense of "Do you desire gods other than Allah as liars?"

**The Qur'anic phrase: ﴿So what is your opinion of the Lord of the worlds?﴾**

That is, what is your opinion of Him when you meet Him, having worshipped other than Him? This is a warning, like His saying: ﴿What has deceived you concerning your Generous Lord?﴾ [al-Infitar: 6]. It has also been said: what delusion has deceived you so that you associated others with Him?

**The Qur'anic phrase: ﴿Then he glanced at the stars, and said, "Indeed, I am sick."﴾**

Ibn Zayd reported from his father: their king sent to him, "Tomorrow is our festival, so come out with us." He looked at a rising star and said, "Indeed, this rises along with my sickness." The science of the stars was in use among them and was studied, so he gave them the impression that he meant it in that sense. He showed them an excuse from their own belief for himself. They were people of herding and farming, and these two livelihoods require looking at the stars.

Ibn 'Abbas said: the science of the stars was from prophethood. When Allah stopped the sun for Yusha' ibn Nun, that knowledge was nullified, so Abraham's looking at them was prophetic knowledge.

Juwaybir related from al-Dahhak: the science of the stars remained until the time of Jesus (peace be upon him). They entered upon him in a place where he could not be seen from it, and Mary said to them, "From where did you know his location?" They said, "From the stars." At that, he prayed to his Lord, "O Allah, do not make them understand its knowledge." So no one knows the science of the stars, and its ruling became forbidden in the Shari'ah, while its knowledge among people became unknown.

Al-Kalbi said: they were in a village between Basra and Kufa called Hurmuzjird. [[Al-Tabari mentions this name in his History, vol. 2, p. 346, Leiden edition, part 1.]] They used to study the stars. This is one view.

Al-Hasan said: the meaning is that when they obligated him to go out with them, he reflected on what he would do. According to this, the meaning is that he looked at what came to his mind as an opinion, that is, what arose for him from it, so he knew that every living thing becomes ill, and he said, "Indeed, I am sick."

Al-Khalil and al-Mubarrad said: it is said of a man who reflects on a matter to plan it, "He looked at the stars."

It was also said: the hour in which they called him to go out with them was an hour in which fever overcame him.

It was also said: the meaning is that he looked at the things that appeared, and knew that they have a creator and manager, and that they change as they change.

**Continuing: ﴿"Indeed, I am sick."﴾**

Al-Dahhak said: the meaning of *saqim* (sick) is "I will become sick with the sickness of death," because whoever is destined to die generally becomes sick and then dies. This is a equivocation and an indirect statement, just as he said to the king when he asked about Sarah, "She is my sister," meaning the brotherhood of faith.

Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak also said: he pointed to them a sickness and illness that is contagious, like the plague, and they used to flee from the plague. ﴿So they turned away from him, retreating﴾ means fleeing from him for fear of contagion.

Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim narrated, saying: my father told us, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad told us, from Asbat, from al-Suddi, from Abu Malik and Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas; and from Samurah, from al-Hamdani, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: They said to Abraham, "We have a festival. If you came out with us, our religion would please you." When the day of the festival came, they went out and he went out with them. When they were on part of the road, he threw himself down and said, "Indeed, I am sick, my leg hurts." They trod on his leg while he was prostrate. When they had gone, he called out after them: ﴿And by Allah, I will surely plot against your idols﴾ [al-Anbiya': 57].

Abu 'Abd Allah (al-Qurtubi) said: this does not contradict what Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr said, because it is possible that two matters came together for him.

I say: In the Sahih, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Abraham the prophet (peace be upon him) told no lies except three lies..." The hadith. This has already passed in Surat al-Anbiya', and it indicates that he was not really sick, but only gave them an indirect hint. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has said: ﴿Indeed, you will die, and indeed they will die﴾ [al-Zumar: 30]. So the meaning is: "I am sick concerning what is to come," but they understood that he was sick at that moment. This is among the equivocations of speech, as we have mentioned. From it is the well-known proverb: "Safety is enough of a disease" [[Al-Daylami narrated it in Musnad al-Firdaws as a hadith from Ibn 'Abbas with a weak chain.]], and the verse of Labid:

*So I called upon my Lord for safety, striving,*
*that He might heal me, and then safety became a disease.*

A man died suddenly, and people gathered around him, saying, "He died while healthy!" A Bedouin said: "Is one healthy in whose neck death is?" So Abraham was truthful, but since the prophets are of close station and chosen, this was counted as a sin for him. For this reason he said: ﴿and the One from whom I hope He will forgive my sin on the Day of Judgment﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 82]. All of this has already been explained in detail, and praise be to Allah. [[See vol. 11, p. 300, and vol. 13, first or second edition.]]

It was also said: he meant "sick in soul" because of their disbelief.

The word *al-nujum* (the stars) may be the plural of *najm* (a star), and it may be a singular verbal noun (*masdar*).

**The Qur'anic phrase: ﴿And indeed, from among his followers was Abraham﴾**

Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, from among the people of his religion. Mujahid said: that is, upon his path and his sunnah (way and practice).

Al-Asma'i said: *al-shi'ah* means the helpers. It is derived from *al-shiya'* (kindling), which is the small wood that is burnt together with large logs until the fire is kindled.

Al-Kalbi and al-Farra' said: the meaning is, "And indeed, from among the followers of Muhammad was Abraham." On this view, the pronoun in *shi'atihi* refers to Muhammad (ﷺ). According to the first view, it refers to Noah, and this is more apparent, because he is the one mentioned first. Between Noah and Abraham there were only two prophets, Hud and Salih. The time between Noah and Abraham was two thousand six hundred and forty years. This is related by al-Zamakhshari.

That is, sincere, free from polytheism and doubt. 'Awf al-A'rabi said: I asked Muhammad ibn Sirin, "What is the sound heart?" He said: "One who gives sincere counsel to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, concerning His creation." Al-Tabari reports from Ghalib al-Qattan, 'Awf and others, from Muhammad ibn Sirin, that he used to say to al-Hajjaj: "Poor Abu Muhammad! If Allah punishes him, it is for his sin; and if He forgives him, then good for him. Even if his heart is sound, one better than him has committed sins." 'Awf said: I said to Muhammad, "What is the sound heart?" He said: "That one knows that Allah is the Truth, that the Hour is coming, and that Allah will resurrect those who are in the graves."

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an) on Surah 37, verses 91–96:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So he turned aside to their gods﴾. Al-Suddi said: "He went to them." Abu Malik said: "He went to them." Abu Malik also said: "He came to them, upon them." It was also said: "He veered." The meanings are close. *Farā'a* (to turn aside) means *yarūgh*, *rawgan* and *rawaghān*, when one inclines. A *ṭarīq rā'igh* is a crooked path. The poet said:

*And he shows you, from the tip of his tongue, sweetness,*
*but he slips away from you as the fox slips away.*

He said: "Will you not eat?" He addressed them as one addresses a rational being, because they had placed them in that rank. Likewise: "What is the matter with you that you do not speak?" It was said: there was food before the idols that they had left so they could eat it when they returned from the festival. They had left it so that the blessing of their idols would reach it, in their belief. It was also said: they left it for the custodians (*sadana*). It was also said: he himself brought food near them, mockingly, and said: "Will you not eat? What is the matter with you that you do not speak?"

﴿Then he turned upon them, striking with the right hand﴾. He specified striking with the right hand because it is the stronger, and striking with it is more forceful. This was said by al-Dahhak and al-Rabi' ibn Anas. It was also said: the "right hand" means the oath he swore when he said: ﴿And by Allah, I will surely plot against your idols﴾ [al-Anbiya: 57]. Al-Farra' and Tha'lab said: "striking with strength," and *al-yamin* means strength. It was also said: "with justice," and *al-yamin* here means justice. From this is the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And if he had invented against Us some sayings, We would have seized him by the right hand﴾ [al-Haqqah: 44–45], meaning with justice. So justice belongs to the right hand, and injustice to the left. Do you not see that the enemy is on the left, sins are on the left, and obedience is on the right? For this reason He said: ﴿You used to come to us from the right﴾ [al-Saffat: 28], meaning from the direction of obedience. So the right hand is the place of justice for the Muslim, and the left is the place of injustice. Do you not see that he pledged allegiance to Allah with his right hand on the Day of the Covenant? So the pledge is with the right hand, and therefore he is given his book tomorrow in his right hand, because he fulfilled the pledge. But the one who breaks the pledge, who flees from Allah with his neck, is given his book in his left hand, because injustice is there. So His words: ﴿Then he turned upon them, striking with the right hand﴾ mean: with that justice upon which he had pledged allegiance to Allah on the Day of the Covenant, and then fulfilled it here.

So he made those idols into *judhadh*, that is, crumbs, like *al-judhadhah*, which is roasted flour (*sawiq*). This is not of the category of strength; it was said by al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim.

﴿Then they came toward him hastening﴾. Hamzah read *yuzaffūn* with a *ḍammah* on the *yā'*. The rest read it with a *fatḥah*, meaning they hasten. This was said by Ibn Zayd. Qatadah and al-Suddi said: they walk. It was also said: the meaning is that they walk gathered together at leisure, secure that anyone might harm their gods. It was also said: the meaning is that they move stealthily, between walking and running, and from it comes *zafīf al-na'āmah* (the swift gliding of the ostrich). Al-Dahhak said: they run. Yahya ibn Salam related: they tremble with anger. It was also said: they strut, which is the walk of pride, said by Mujahid. From it comes *zifāf al-'arūs ilā zawjihā* (the bride's procession to her husband). Al-Farazdaq said:

*And the stallion of the herd came before its young camels,*
*and it came hastening, and the she-camels came behind it, moving swiftly.*

[Footnote: *Al-qarī'*: the stallion chosen for mating. *Al-shawl* (sing. *shā'ilah*): she-camels whose time, carrying or birth, has passed seven months so their milk has dried up. *Iflāluhā*: their young. *Yazuff*: runs. He means that the stallion flees from the intensity of the cold, and likewise the young camels.]

As for the one who reads *yuzaffūn*, its meaning is that they cause others to hasten, that is, they carry them to be hurried along. In this case the object is omitted. Al-Asma'i said: *azafftu al-ibil* means I carried the camels so that they would hasten. It was also said: both are dialects; it is said *zaffa al-qawm* and *azaffū* (the people hastened), *zaffaftu al-'arūs*, *azfaftuhā* and *izdaffaftuhā* with the same meaning. *Al-muzaffah* is the litter in which the bride is carried in procession. This was related from al-Khalil.

Al-Nahhas said: "*Yuzaffūn*" with a *ḍammah* on the *yā'*. Abu Hatim claimed that he did not know this dialect, though a group of scholars knew it, among them al-Farra', who likened it to their saying: *atradtu al-rajul*, meaning I brought him to that state, and *taradtuhu*, meaning I removed him. He and others recited:

*Husayn desired to lead the *judha'ah*,*
*but Husayn became humiliated and oppressed.*

[Footnote: The verse is by al-Mukhabbal al-Sa'di, satirizing al-Zibriqan and his people, who were known as al-Judha'. Al-Asma'i narrated it, as in *al-Lisan* under *q-h-r*, as *qad udhilla wa uqhira* with the passive form, meaning his affair ended in humiliation and subjugation.]

That is, he was brought to that state, and so *yuzaffūn* means they are brought to hastening. Muhammad ibn Zayd said: *al-zafif* is speed. Abu Ishaq said: *al-zafif* is the first running of the ostrich. Abu Hatim said: al-Kisa'i claimed that some people recited ﴿*fa-aqbalū ilayhi yazifūn*﴾ with a light pronunciation, from *wazafa yazifu*, like *wazana yazinu*. Al-Nahhas said: this is Abu Hatim's report, and Abu Hatim did not hear anything from al-Kisa'i. Al-Farra', who was the companion of al-Kisa'i, related from al-Kisa'i that he did not know *yazifūn* with a light pronunciation. Al-Farra' said: "I also do not know it." Abu Ishaq said: others besides them have made it known, namely that it is said *wazafa yazifu* (or *yazuffu*) when he hastened. Al-Nahhas said: we do not know of anyone who recited *yazifūn*. I say: it is the recitation of Abdullah ibn Yazid, as al-Mahdawi mentioned. Al-Zamakhshari said: *yuzaffūn* is in the passive voice, and *yuzfūn* is from *zafāhu*, when he drove him on, as if some of them drive others because of their haste toward him. Al-Tha'labi mentioned from al-Hasan, Mujahid and Ibn al-Sumayqa *yarfūn* with a *rā'*, from *rafīf al-na'am*, which is running between walking and flying.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He said: Do you worship what you carve?﴾ There is an omission in it, meaning they said: "Who did this to our gods?" Then he said, arguing: "Do you worship what you carve?" meaning: do you worship idols that you carve with your own hands, shaping them? *Al-naḥt* is carving and shaping; he carved it, *yanḥituhu* with a *kasrah*, *naḥtan*, meaning he shaped it. *Al-nuḥātah* is shavings, and *al-minḥat* is that with which something is carved.

﴿And Allah created you and what you make﴾. "*Mā*" is in the accusative position, meaning and He created what you make of the idols, namely wood, stones and other things, as in His words: ﴿Rather, your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, who originated them﴾ [al-Anbiya: 56]. It was also said: "*mā*" is interrogative, and its meaning is to belittle their work. It was also said: it is negation, and the meaning is: "You do not make that; rather, Allah is its creator." The best view is that "*mā*" with the verb is a verbal noun, and the sense is: "Allah created you and your work." This is the doctrine of the People of the Sunnah: that actions are created by Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and acquired by the servants. In this is a refutation of the doctrines of the Qadariyyah and the Jabriyyah.

Abu Hurayrah related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Indeed Allah is the creator of every craftsman and his craft." Al-Tha'labi mentioned it. Al-Bayhaqi narrated it from the hadith of Hudhayfah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, made every maker and his making. He is the Creator and He is the Maker, glory be to Him." We have explained both in the book *al-Asna fi Sharh Asma' Allah al-Husna*.

[Footnote: *Al-qarī'*: the stallion chosen for mating. *Al-shawl* (sing. *shā'ilah*): she-camels whose time, carrying or birth, has passed seven months so their milk has dried up. *Iflāluhā*: their young. *Yazuff*: runs. He means that the stallion flees from the intensity of the cold, and likewise the young camels.]

As for the one who reads *yuzaffūn*, its meaning is that they cause others to hasten, that is, they carry them to be hurried along. In this case the object is omitted. Al-Asma'i said: *azafftu al-ibil* means I carried the camels so that they would hasten. It was also said: both are dialects; it is said *zaffa al-qawm* and *azaffū* (the people hastened), *zaffaftu al-'arūs*, *azfaftuhā* and *izdaffaftuhā* with the same meaning. *Al-muzaffah* is the litter in which the bride is carried in procession. This was related from al-Khalil.

Al-Nahhas said: "*Yuzaffūn*" with a *ḍammah* on the *yā'*. Abu Hatim claimed that he did not know this dialect, though a group of scholars knew it, among them al-Farra', who likened it to their saying: *atradtu al-rajul*, meaning I brought him to that state, and *taradtuhu*, meaning I removed him. He and others recited:

*Husayn desired to lead the *judha'ah*,*
*but Husayn became humiliated and oppressed.*

[Footnote: The verse is by al-Mukhabbal al-Sa'di, satirizing al-Zibriqan and his people, who were known as al-Judha'. Al-Asma'i narrated it, as in *al-Lisan* under *q-h-r*, as *qad udhilla wa uqhira* with the passive form, meaning his affair ended in humiliation and subjugation.]

That is, he was brought to that state, and so *yuzaffūn* means they are brought to hastening. Muhammad ibn Zayd said: *al-zafif* is speed. Abu Ishaq said: *al-zafif* is the first running of the ostrich. Abu Hatim said: al-Kisa'i claimed that some people recited ﴿*fa-aqbalū ilayhi yazifūn*﴾ with a light pronunciation, from *wazafa yazifu*, like *wazana yazinu*. Al-Nahhas said: this is Abu Hatim's report, and Abu Hatim did not hear anything from al-Kisa'i. Al-Farra', who was the companion of al-Kisa'i, related from al-Kisa'i that he did not know *yazifūn* with a light pronunciation. Al-Farra' said: "I also do not know it." Abu Ishaq said: others besides them have made it known, namely that it is said *wazafa yazifu* (or *yazuffu*) when he hastened. Al-Nahhas said: we do not know of anyone who recited *yazifūn*. I say: it is the recitation of Abdullah ibn Yazid, as al-Mahdawi mentioned. Al-Zamakhshari said: *yuzaffūn* is in the passive voice, and *yuzfūn* is from *zafāhu*, when he drove him on, as if some of them drive others because of their haste toward him. Al-Tha'labi mentioned from al-Hasan, Mujahid and Ibn al-Sumayqa *yarfūn* with a *rā'*, from *rafīf al-na'am*, which is running between walking and flying.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He said: Do you worship what you carve?﴾ There is an omission in it, meaning they said: "Who did this to our gods?" Then he said, arguing: "Do you worship what you carve?" meaning: do you worship idols that you carve with your own hands, shaping them? *Al-naḥt* is carving and shaping; he carved it, *yanḥituhu* with a *kasrah*, *naḥtan*, meaning he shaped it. *Al-nuḥātah* is shavings, and *al-minḥat* is that with which something is carved.

﴿And Allah created you and what you make﴾. "*Mā*" is in the accusative position, meaning and He created what you make of the idols, namely wood, stones and other things, as in His words: ﴿Rather, your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, who originated them﴾ [al-Anbiya: 56]. It was also said: "*mā*" is interrogative, and its meaning is to belittle their work. It was also said: it is negation, and the meaning is: "You do not make that; rather, Allah is its creator." The best view is that "*mā*" with the verb is a verbal noun, and the sense is: "Allah created you and your work." This is the doctrine of the People of the Sunnah: that actions are created by Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and acquired by the servants. In this is a refutation of the doctrines of the Qadariyyah and the Jabriyyah.

Abu Hurayrah related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Indeed Allah is the creator of every craftsman and his craft." Al-Tha'labi mentioned it. Al-Bayhaqi narrated it from the hadith of Hudhayfah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, made every maker and his making. He is the Creator and He is the Maker, glory be to Him." We have explained both in the book *al-Asna fi Sharh Asma' Allah al-Husna*.

It was also said: "He veered." The meanings are close. *Farā'a* (to turn aside) means *yarūgh*, *rawgan* and *rawaghān*, when one inclines. A *ṭarīq rā'igh* is a crooked path. The poet said:

*And he shows you, from the tip of his tongue, sweetness,*
*but he slips away from you as the fox slips away.*

He said: "Will you not eat?" He addressed them as one addresses a rational being, because they had placed them in that rank. Likewise: "What is the matter with you that you do not speak?" It was said: there was food before the idols that they had left so they could eat it when they returned from the festival. They had left it so that the blessing of their idols would reach it, in their belief. It was also said: they left it for the custodians (*sadana*). It was also said: he himself brought food near them, mockingly, and said: "Will you not eat? What is the matter with you that you do not speak?"

﴿Then he turned upon them, striking with the right hand﴾. He specified striking with the right hand because it is the stronger, and striking with it is more forceful. This was said by al-Dahhak and al-Rabi' ibn Anas. It was also said: the "right hand" means the oath he swore when he said: ﴿And by Allah, I will surely plot against your idols﴾ [al-Anbiya: 57]. So the pledge is with the right hand, and therefore he is given his book tomorrow in his right hand, because he fulfilled the pledge. But the one who breaks the pledge, who flees from Allah with his neck, is given his book in his left hand, because injustice is there. So His words: ﴿Then he turned upon them, striking with the right hand﴾ mean: with that justice upon which he had pledged allegiance to Allah on the Day of the Covenant, and then fulfilled it here.

*And the stallion of the herd came before its young camels,*

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 37, verse 97–98:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They said, "Build for him a structure"﴾, meaning: they consulted about his affair after he had overcome them with proof, as already explained in "al-Anbiya'" [[See vol. 11, p. 303 of the first or second edition.]]. Their statement, "Build for him a structure," means: you shall fill it with firewood and set it alight, then cast him into it, and it is the Hell-fire (al-Jahim).

Ibn Abbas said: They built a wall of stone whose height in the sky was thirty cubits, and they filled it with fire and threw him into it.

Ibn Amr ibn al-As said: When he was inside the structure, he said: "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs" (ﷺ not applicable). 

The definite article in "al-Jahim" indicates a reference, meaning: in its Hell-fire, that is, in the Hell-fire of that structure.

al-Tabari mentioned that the name of the one who said this was al-Haymazan [[It was mentioned in vol. 11, p. 303 that his name was Hayzar.]], a man from the Arabs of Persia, who are the Turks, and he is the one about whom the hadith came: "While a man was walking in his garment, admiring himself in it, he was swallowed up by the earth, and he continues to sink into the earth until the Day of Resurrection." And Allah knows best.

﴿So they intended a scheme against him﴾, meaning against Abraham. Kayd means plotting, that is, they devised means to destroy him.

﴿So We made them the lowest﴾, meaning the subdued and defeated, since his proof prevailed in a way they could not repel, and their plotting and scheming did not take effect against him.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 37, verse 99–101:

﴿So We gave him the good news of a forbearing boy.﴾ In this there are two issues.

The first: this verse is a basis for hijrah (emigration) and 'uzlah (withdrawal from people). The first to do so was Ibrahim, peace be upon him, when Allah rescued him from the fire. ﴿He said: "Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me."﴾ That is, I am emigrating from the land of my people and my birthplace to where I can worship my Lord, for He will guide me in what I intend to the right course. Muqatil said: he was the first of creation to emigrate, along with Lut and Sarah, to the Holy Land, which is the land of al-Sham. It was also said: "I am going with my works and my worship, and my heart and my intention." According to this view, his going was with his deeds, not with his body. The explanation of this has already passed in [al-Kahf [[See vol. 10, p. 36 and following, first or second edition.]]] in full. And according to the first view, it refers to emigration to al-Sham and Bayt al-Maqdis.

It was also said: he went out to Harran and stayed there for a period. Then it was said: he said this to those who had separated from his people, so it would be a rebuke to them. It was also said: he said it to those among his family who emigrated with him, so it would be an encouragement from him. It was also said: he said this before being cast into the fire. On this view there are two interpretations. One: "I am going to what my Lord has decreed for me." The second: "I am going to die," just as one says of someone who has died, "He has gone to Allah, the Exalted," because he, peace be upon him, imagined that he would die by being cast into the fire, given the known nature of the fire in destroying what is thrown into it, until it was said to it: ﴿O fire, be cool and safe.﴾ At that point Ibrahim was saved from it. And regarding His words "He will guide me" on this view, there are two interpretations: one, "He will guide me" to deliverance from it; the second, to Paradise.

Sulayman ibn Surad, who was among those who met the Prophet ﷺ, said: When they intended to cast Ibrahim into the fire, they began gathering firewood for him. An old woman would carry it on her back and say: "I am taking it to this one who mentions our gods." When he was taken to be thrown into the fire, ﴿he said: "Indeed, I am going to my Lord."﴾ When he was cast into the fire, he said: (Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs). Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿O fire, be cool and safe﴾ [al-Anbiya: 69]. Abu Lut, who was his cousin, said: "Indeed, the fire did not burn him because of his kinship to me." So Allah sent a flame of fire and it burned him.

The second issue: His words, the Exalted: ﴿My Lord, grant me [a child] from among the righteous.﴾ When Allah informed him that He would deliver him, he prayed to Allah that He would support him with a child with whom he would find companionship in his estrangement. The discussion of this has already passed in [Al 'Imran [[See vol. 4, p. 73, first or second edition.]]]. In the speech there is an omission, meaning: grant me a righteous child from among the righteous, and omission of this kind is common. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿So We gave him the good news of a forbearing boy.﴾ That is, he will be forbearing in his old age, so he was given the good news that this child would survive, because a young child is not described by that. The good news came through the tongues of the angels, as has preceded in [Hud [[See vol. 9, p. 62, first or second edition.]]]. It will also come in [al-Dhariyat [[In the explanation of verse 28 of the said surah.]]].
