The seventh issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾. Dhibh (ذِبْح) is the name of what is slaughtered, and its plural is dhubuh, like tihn (طِحْن) being the name of what is ground. Al-dhabh (ذَبْح) with a fatha is the verbal noun. "Azim" means great in rank, not great in body. Its rank became great because the one slaughtered was ransomed by it, or because it was accepted. Al-Nahhas said: "Azim in the language is used for the large and for the noble. The people of tafsir hold that here it means the noble, or the accepted." Ibn Abbas said: it was the ram with which Habil drew near (to God), and it was in Paradise grazing until God ransomed Isma'il with it. He also said: it was a ram sent by God from Paradise which had grazed in Paradise for forty autumns. Al-Hasan said: Isma'il was only ransomed with a mountain antelope (ar-arwa) that descended upon him from Thabir, and Ibrahim slaughtered it as a ransom for his son; this is also the view of Ali, may Allah be pleased with him. When Ibrahim saw it, he took it, slaughtered it, and freed his son, and said: "O my son, today you have been given to me." Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: it has been said that he was ransomed with a wa'l (ibex), and the wa'l is the mountain he-goat. But the people of tafsir hold that he was ransomed with a ram.

The eighth issue: In this verse there is evidence that sacrificing sheep is better than camels and cattle. This is the position of Malik and his companions. They said: the best sacrificial animals are male sheep (fuhul al-danh), female sheep are better than a male goat, male goats are better than female goats, and female goats are better than camels and cattle. Their proof is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾, meaning large of body and fat, and that is a ram, not a camel nor a cow. Mujahid and others narrated from Ibn Abbas that a man asked him: "I have vowed to slaughter my son?" He said: "A fat ram will suffice you," then he recited: ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾. Some of them said: "If God knew of an animal better than the ram, He would have ransomed Isaac with it." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) sacrificed two white horned rams (kabshayn amlahayn). Most of what he sacrificed were rams. Ibn Abi Shaybah mentioned, from Ibn Ulayyah, from al-Layth, from Mujahid, who said: "The great sacrifice is the sheep."

The ninth issue: They differed as to which is better: the udhiyya (sacrifice) or giving its price in charity. Malik and his companions said: the sacrifice is better, except at Mina, because it is not the place of sacrifice; Abu Umar related this. Ibn al-Mundhir said: it was narrated to us from Bilal that he said: "I do not mind whether I sacrifice except with your (animal)... and that I place it on an orphan who has been dusted by it" (thus said the muhaddith) "is dearer to me than that I sacrifice with it." This is the view of al-Sha'bi that charity is better. Malik and Abu Thawr also held this. There is a second view: that the sacrifice is better; this is the view of Rabi'a and Abu al-Zinad, and Ashab al-Ra'y hold it too. Abu Umar and Ahmad ibn Hanbal added: they said the sacrifice is better than charity, because the sacrifice is a confirmed sunnah like the Eid prayer, and it is known that the Eid prayer is better than all other voluntary prayers, and likewise the sunnah prayers are better than all voluntary acts. Abu Umar said: fine reports have been transmitted concerning the virtue of sacrifices, among them what Sa'id ibn Dawud ibn Abi Zanbar narrated from Malik, from Thawr ibn Zayd, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "There is no expenditure after maintaining kinship ties more excellent with God than shedding blood." Abu Umar said: this is a gharib hadith from the hadith of Malik. And from Aisha, who said: "O people, sacrifice and be content of soul, for I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: 'No servant who turns his sacrifice toward the qiblah but its blood, its horns and its wool will be good deeds placed in his scale on the Day of Resurrection; for if the blood falls on the earth, it falls within the protection of God until it is repaid to its owner on the Day of Resurrection.'" Abu Umar mentioned it in the Kitab al-Tamhid. Al-Tirmidhi also narrated from her that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "No son of Adam has done any deed on the day of sacrifice more beloved to God than shedding blood; it comes on the Day of Resurrection with its horns, hair and hooves, and the blood reaches a place with God before it falls to the earth, so be content of soul with it." He said: and on this subject there are reports from Imran ibn Husayn and Zayd ibn Arqam. This is a hasan hadith.

The tenth issue: The sacrifice is not obligatory, but it is a sunnah, and it is well known. Ikrimah said: Ibn Abbas used to send me on the day of al-Adha with two dirhams to buy meat for him, and he would say: "Whomever you meet, say: this is the sacrifice of Ibn Abbas." Abu Umar said: the explanation of this and what is narrated of Abu Bakr and Umar, that they did not sacrifice, according to the scholars, is so that constant performance of it would not lead people to believe it is an obligatory duty; and they were imams whom those after them followed in their religion, because they were the intermediaries between the Prophet (ﷺ) and his community, so they had latitude in ijtihad in this matter that is not permitted to others today. And

Al-Tahawi related in his Mukhtasar: Abu Hanifa said: The sacrifice (udhiyah) is obligatory for resident, well-off people from the cities, and it is not obligatory for the traveller. He said: A man is obliged to sacrifice on behalf of his young child just as he is obliged to sacrifice on his own behalf. Abu Yusuf and Muhammad disagreed with him and said: It is not obligatory, but it is a sunnah (recommended practice), and whoever is able to do it is not excused from abandoning it. He said: And this is what we adopt. Abu Umar said: This is also the view of Malik, who said: No one should abandon it, whether travelling or resident. If he abandons it, he has done something wrong, unless he has an excuse, except for the pilgrim at Mina. Al-Shafi'i said: It is a sunnah for all people, and for the pilgrim at Mina, and it is not obligatory. Those who made it obligatory argued that the Prophet ﷺ commanded Abu Burda ibn Niyar to repeat the sacrifice with another animal, because what is not an obligation (fard) would not require a repetition. Others argued with the hadith of Umm Salama from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "When the ten days begin and one of you intends to sacrifice..." They said: If it were obligatory, it would not have been made dependent on the intention of the one sacrificing. This is also the view of Abu Bakr, Umar, Abu Mas'ud al-Badri and Bilal.

Eleventh: By the consensus (ijma', scholarly agreement) of the Muslims, what is sacrificed consists of the eight pairs: sheep, goats, camels and cattle. Ibn al-Mundhir said: It has been reported from al-Hasan ibn Salih that he said: A wild cow may be sacrificed for seven people, and a gazelle for one man. Al-Shafi'i said: If a wild bull mounts a domestic cow, or a domestic bull mounts a wild cow, none of their offspring is valid as a sacrifice. The people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y) said: It is permissible, because its offspring has the status of its mother. Abu Thawr said: It is permissible if it is attributed to the livestock (al-an'am).

Twelfth: The discussion of the time of slaughter and of eating from the sacrifice has already been covered fully in Surat al-Hajj.[[See vol. 12, p. 42 onward, first or second edition.]] In Sahih Muslim, from Anas, who said: "The Prophet ﷺ sacrificed two white rams with horns, which he slaughtered with his own hand, saying the name of God and proclaiming takbir, and he placed his foot on their necks." In one narration he said: "He would say: In the name of God, God is greatest." Hadith of Imran ibn Husayn was mentioned at the end of Surat al-An'am,[[See vol. 7, p. 155, first or second edition.]] and the discussion of dhakah (ritual slaughter), its explanation, and what may be slaughtered with, and that the slaughter of the fetus is the slaughter of its mother, was covered fully in Surat al-Ma'idah.[[See vol. 6, p. 50 onward, first or second edition.]] In Sahih Muslim, from Aisha, that the Messenger of God ﷺ "commanded a horned ram that walks in black, kneels in black and looks in black to be brought so that he might sacrifice it." He said to her: "O Aisha, bring me the knife," then said: "Sharpen it on a stone," and she did so. Then he took it and took the ram, laid it down and slaughtered it, then said: "In the name of God. O God, accept from Muhammad, the family of Muhammad, and the community of Muhammad," and then he sacrificed it. The scholars differed on this. Al-Hasan al-Basri used to say at the sacrifice: "In the name of God, God is greatest; this is from you and for you; accept from so-and-so." Malik said: If he does that, it is good, and if he does not do it but mentions God's name, it suffices him. Al-Shafi'i said: The invocation over the slaughtered animal is "In the name of God." If he adds something after that of the remembrance of God, or invokes blessings upon Muhammad, peace be upon him, I do not dislike it; or if he says: "O God, accept from me," or "accept from so-and-so," there is no harm. Al-Nu'man (Abu Hanifa) said: It is disliked to mention anything other than God's name with it; it is disliked to say: "O God, accept from so-and-so" at the time of slaughter. He said: There is no harm if it is before the invocation and before laying the animal down for slaughter. The hadith of Aisha refutes this view. It has already been mentioned that Ibrahim, peace be upon him, when he intended to slaughter his son, said: "God is greatest, and praise be to God," and so it remained a sunnah.

Thirteenth: Al-Bara' ibn Azib narrated that the Messenger of God ﷺ was asked: What should be avoided in sacrificial animals? He gestured with his hand and said: "Four" (Al-Bara' used to gesture with his hand and say: My hand is shorter than the hand of the Messenger of God ﷺ): "The lame whose limp is evident, the one-eyed whose blindness is evident, the sick whose illness is evident, and the emaciated that has no marrow." The wording is that of Malik, and there is no disagreement about it, but there is disagreement about minor cases of these. In al-Tirmidhi, from Ali, may God be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ commanded us to examine (nastashrif) the eyes and ears [[nastashrif: that is, to look at and examine them, so that there is no defect in them.]], and that we should not sacrifice an animal with a cut ear from the front (muqabalah), nor one cut from behind (mudabarah), nor one with a split ear (sharqa'), nor one with a hole in the ear (kharqa'). He said: Al-Muqabalah is one whose ear tip is cut off, al-Mudabarah is one cut from the side of the ear, al-Sharqa' is one whose ear is split, and al-Kharqa' is one whose ear is pierced. He said: This is a hasan sahih hadith. In the Muwatta', from Nafi', that Abdullah ibn Umar used to avoid sacrificial animals and camels that had not grown their teeth (lam tusnan) and those with some deficiency in their bodies. Malik said: This is the most beloved of what I have heard to me. Al-Qutabi said: Lam tusnan means its teeth had not grown, as if it had not been given teeth. This is like saying: So-and-so was not given milk (lam yulban), meaning he was not given milk; and he was not given ghee (lam yusman), meaning he was not given ghee; and he was not given honey (lam yu'sal), meaning he was not given honey. [[Ibn Manzur, in Lisan al-Arab under the root "s-n-n," commented on al-Qutabi's narration and explanation, saying: "Al-Qutabi erred both in the narration and in the explanation, because he narrated the hadith as 'lam tusnan' with the first nun vowelled with a fatha, whereas he memorized it from a narrator who did not vowel it, while the people of precision and vocalization narrated it as 'lam tusinn' with a kasra on the nun, which is the correct form in Arabic. The meaning is 'lam tusan,' and the doubling is made apparent because the final nun is sukun, as one says: 'lam yujall.' Ibn Umar meant that he sacrificed an animal that had not reached the age of 'thaniyyah' (two front teeth), that is, had not become a thaniyyah; and when it has become a thaniyyah, it has become musinn. Then he said: As for al-Qutabi's error in the other respect, his saying: 'sannat al-badanah' when its teeth grew and 'sannaha Allah' is not correct, and his saying: 'lam yulban wa lam yusman,' meaning it was not given milk and ghee, is not correct; rather, they mean it was not fed ghee and was not given milk to drink."]] This is like the prohibition in sacrificial animals against the hatma' (one with broken or missing front teeth). Abu Umar said: According to Malik there is no harm in sacrificing a hatma' sheep if the loss of its teeth is due to old age and senility, and it is fat; but if its teeth are missing while it is young, it is not permissible to sacrifice it, because it is a serious defect. Every deficiency is disliked, and its explanation and detail are in the books of fiqh (jurisprudence). It is reported from the Prophet ﷺ: "Examine your sacrificial animals carefully, for they will be your mounts over the Sirat (bridge)." Al-Zamakhshari mentioned it.

Fourteenth: The verse indicates that whoever vows to slaughter his son or to make a dhibh (slaughter) of him must redeem him with a ram, just as Ibrahim redeemed his son with it, said Ibn Abbas. From him there is another narration: He should slaughter a hundred camels, just as Abd al-Muttalib redeemed his son with them. Al-Sha'bi narrated both reports from him. Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad narrated from him: It suffices him as an expiation for an oath. Masruq said: He owes nothing. Al-Shafi'i said: It is a sin, for which he should seek God's forgiveness. Abu Hanifa said: It is an expression by which he is obliged to slaughter a sheep regarding his son, and he is not obliged to anything regarding someone other than his son. Muhammad said: Regarding swearing by slaughtering his slave, he is subject to the same as regarding swearing by slaughtering his son, if he breaks the oath. Ibn Abd al-Hakam reported from Malik regarding one who said: "I will slaughter my son at the Station of Ibrahim" in an oath, then broke it: he owes a hady (offering). He said: Whoever vows to slaughter his son without saying "at the Station of Ibrahim" and without intending it, there is nothing owed by him. He said: Whoever makes his son a hady, he gives a hady on his behalf. Al-Qadi Ibn al-Arabi said: He is obliged to a sheep, as Abu Hanifa said, because God, exalted is He, made the slaughter of the son an expression for the slaughter of a sheep according to the law, so God obligated Ibrahim to slaughter the son, and removed that from him by slaughtering a sheep. Likewise, if a slave vows to slaughter his son, he is obliged to slaughter a sheep, because God, exalted is He, said: ﴿the religion of your father Ibrahim﴾ [al-Hajj: 78], and faith is a fundamental commitment, while a vow is a secondary commitment, so it must be understood in light of it. If it is said: How can Ibrahim be commanded to slaughter the son when it is a sin, and a command to sin is not permissible? We say: This is an objection to the Book of God, and this would not come from one who believes in Islam, so how about one who gives legal rulings on the lawful and the unlawful, when God, exalted is He, has said: "Do what you are commanded."

Al-Qurtubi said: What clears the confusion from people's hearts on this point is that acts of disobedience (ma'asi) and acts of obedience (ta'at) are not inherent attributes of things themselves. Rather, obedience is the name for those actions to which a command (amr) has been attached, and disobedience is the name for those actions to which a prohibition (nahy) has been attached. So when the command was attached to the slaughter of the son Isma'il by Ibrahim, it became an act of obedience and a trial. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: "Indeed, this is the clear trial" concerning patience in slaughtering the son and the self. When the prohibition was attached to us regarding the slaughter of our sons, it became disobedience.

If it is asked: How can it become a vow (nadhr) when it is disobedience? We answer: It would only be disobedience if he intended to slaughter the son through his vow and did not intend the ransom (fida'). If it is asked: What if it occurred and he intended the disobedience and did not intend the ransom? We answer: If he intended that, it would not harm his intention and would not affect his vow, because the vow of the son had become an expression for the slaughter of a sheep according to the Law (shar'an).

The fifteenth issue: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We left for him among later generations﴾, meaning: for Ibrahim, a good praise among the nations after him, so that there is no nation but that it sends blessings upon him and loves him. It was also said: it is the supplication of Ibrahim, peace be upon him: "And make for me a tongue of truthfulness among later generations" [al-Shu'ara: 84]. ʿIkrimah said: it is the greeting upon Ibrahim, meaning a greeting from us. It was also said: it is safety for him from calamities, like: ﴿Peace upon Nuh among the worlds﴾ [al-Saffat: 79], as mentioned earlier. "Thus do We reward the doers of good. Indeed, he was among Our believing servants" means: among those who gave servitude (ʿubudiyyah) its due, until they deserved to be attributed to Allah the Exalted.

The sixteenth issue: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We gave him good news of Ishaq, a prophet from among the righteous﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: he was given good news of his prophethood, and he held that the glad tidings occurred twice. [In the margin of al-Jamal, quoting al-Qurtubi: he was given good news of his prophethood, and the glad tidings concerning him occurred twice.] According to this, the one slaughtered is Ishaq, who was given good news of his prophethood as a reward for his patience, his contentment with his Lord's command, and his submission to Him. "And We blessed him and Ishaq": meaning We doubled the favour upon both of them. It was also said: We multiplied their offspring, meaning We blessed Ibrahim and his children, and Ishaq, when He brought forth the prophets of the Children of Israel from his loins.

It has been said that the pronoun in "upon him" returns to Isma'il, and that he is the one slaughtered. Al-Mufaddal said: The sound view that the Qur'an indicates is that it is Isma'il, because He related the story of the one slaughtered, and when He said at the end of the story: "And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice," then said: "Peace upon Ibrahim. Thus do We reward the doers of good," He said: "And We gave him good news of Ishaq, a prophet from among the righteous. And We blessed him" meaning upon Isma'il "and upon Ishaq," he referred to him by a pronoun, because his mention had already preceded. Then He said: "And among their descendants," which indicates that the descendants are those of Isma'il and Ishaq. The narrators do not differ that Isma'il was thirteen years older than Ishaq.

I say: We have mentioned earlier what indicates that Ishaq was older than Isma'il, and that the one given glad tidings is Ishaq by the explicit text of the revelation. When the glad tidings of Ishaq are explicit, then the one slaughtered is without doubt Ishaq. Ibrahim was given glad tidings of him twice: the first by his birth, and the second by his prophethood, as Ibn ʿAbbas said. Prophethood only occurs in old age. The word "nabiyyan" (نَبِيًّا) is in the accusative as a state (ḥal), and the pronoun in "upon him" refers to Ibrahim, and there is no mention of Isma'il in the verse so that the pronoun could return to him.

As for what was narrated through the chain of Mu'awiyah, who said: I heard a man say to the Prophet ﷺ: "O son of the two sacrificed ones!" and the Prophet ﷺ laughed. Then Mu'awiyah said: When ʿAbd al-Muttalib dug the well of Zamzam, he vowed to Allah that if He made its matter easy for him, he would surely slaughter one of his sons for Allah. Allah made its matter easy for him, and the arrow fell upon ʿAbd Allah. His maternal uncles, the Banu Makhzum, prevented him and said: Ransom your son. So he ransomed him with a hundred camels, and he was the one slaughtered, while Isma'il is the second one slaughtered. There is no proof in this, because its chain is not established, as we have mentioned in the book al-A'lam concerning the knowledge of the birth of the Chosen One, upon him be blessings and peace. Also, the Arabs call the paternal uncle a father. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They said: We shall worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq﴾ [al-Baqarah: 133], and He said: ﴿And he raised his parents upon the throne﴾ [Yusuf: 100], and they were his father and his maternal aunt. Likewise is what was narrated from the poet al-Farazdaq, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet ﷺ: even if its chain were sound, how much more so, since there is criticism of al-Farazdaq himself.

The seventeenth issue: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And among their descendants are the doer of good and the one who wrongs himself﴾. When He mentioned the blessing in the offspring and their abundance, He said: among them is the good-doer and among them is the wrongdoer. Indeed, the wrongdoer is not benefited by being a son of prophethood. So the Jews and Christians, even if they are of the offspring of Ishaq, and the Arabs, even if they are of the offspring of Isma'il, there must be a distinction between the good-doer and the wrongdoer, and between the believer and the disbeliever. In the revelation: ﴿The Jews and the Christians said: We are the sons of Allah and His beloved﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 18], to the end of the verse, meaning: the sons of the messengers of Allah, so they regarded themselves as superior. This has already been discussed [See vol. 6, p. 12, first or second edition].

Seventeen issues.

The first issue: God's words, ﴿When he reached the age of striving with him﴾, meaning: So We gave him the boy, and when he reached the stage of running about with his father, helping him in his worldly affairs, ﴿he said: "O my son, I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you."﴾

Mujahid said: "﴿When he reached the age of striving with him﴾" means he grew up and attained the striving of Abraham (his father). Al-Farra' said: He was thirteen years old that day. Ibn 'Abbas said: It refers to reaching puberty (ihtilam). Qatadah said: He walked with his father. Al-Hasan and Muqatil said: It is the striving of intellect by which the proof is established. Ibn Zayd said: It is striving in worship. Ibn 'Abbas also said: He fasted and prayed. Do you not hear God, Mighty and Majestic, say: ﴿And strove for it its striving﴾ [al-Isra' 17:19]?

The scholars differed about who was commanded to be slaughtered. Most of them said: the one to be slaughtered was Isaac. Among those who said so was al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, and his son 'Abd Allah, and this is the sound position attributed to him. Al-Thawri and Ibn Jurayj traced it back to Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The one to be slaughtered was Isaac. This is also the sound position reported from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, that a man said to him: "O son of the noble elders!" and 'Abd Allah said: "That is Joseph son of Jacob son of Isaac, the sacrificed one of God, son of Abraham, the friend of God," ﷺ.

Hammad ibn Zayd traced it back to the Messenger of God ﷺ, who said: "Indeed the noble one, son of the noble one, son of the noble one, son of the noble one is Joseph son of Jacob son of Isaac son of Abraham, may God bless them all and grant them peace." Abu al-Zubayr narrated from Jabir, who said: The sacrificed one is Isaac. This is also reported from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him. And from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar: that the sacrificed one is Isaac. This is also the view of 'Umar, may God be pleased with him. These are seven of the Companions.

Among the Successors and others who held this view were 'Alqamah, al-Sha'bi, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ka'b al-Ahbar, Qatadah, Masruq, Ikrimah, al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazzah, 'Ata', Muqatil, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit [[In al-Tahdhib, Ibn Abi Khaythamah said: I heard Ibn Ma'in say: "'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Sabit," and whoever says "'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit" has erred; al-Bukhari also mentioned it this way. There is disagreement about the name of his father.]], al-Zuhri, al-Suddi, 'Abd Allah ibn Abi al-Hudhayl and Malik ibn Anas. All of them said: The sacrificed one is Isaac. This is the position of the People of the Two Scriptures, the Jews and the Christians, and a number of scholars chose it, including al-Nahhas [[In another copy: al-Naqqash.]] and al-Tabari and others.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Abraham was shown in a dream the slaughter of Isaac, so he set out with him, a month's journey in a single morning, until he brought him to the place of sacrifice at Mina. When God turned the slaughter away from him and commanded him to sacrifice the ram, he sacrificed it, and he travelled back a month's journey in a single afternoon, the valleys and mountains being folded up for him.

This view is stronger in transmission from the Prophet ﷺ, from the Companions and from the Successors.

Others said: It was Ishmael. Among those who said so were Abu Hurayrah and Abu al-Tufayl 'Amir ibn Wathilah. This was also reported from Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas, and among the Successors: Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Sha'bi, Yusuf ibn Mihran, Mujahid, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, al-Kalbi and 'Alqamah.

Abu Sa'id al-Darir was asked about the sacrificed one, and he recited:

"Indeed the sacrificed one, you were guided, is Ishmael, and the Scripture and the Revelation attest to it.
It is a distinction by which God singled out our Prophet, and the exegesis and the interpretation have brought it.
If you are his community, then do not deny it for him, and the distinction that preference has granted him is a honour."

From al-Asma'i, who said: I asked Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' about the sacrificed one, and he said: "O Asma'i, where has your reason wandered off! When was Isaac in Mecca? It was Ishmael who was in Mecca, and he who built the House with his father, and the place of sacrifice is in Mecca." It was also reported from the Prophet ﷺ: "The sacrificed one is Ishmael." But the first view is more widely transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ, from his Companions and from the Successors.

Those who held that it was Isaac argued that God said that Abraham left his people, emigrated to Syria with his wife Sarah and his nephew Lot, and said: ﴿"Indeed I am going to my Lord; He will guide me."﴾ [al-Saffat 37:99] He supplicated and said: ﴿"My Lord, grant me of the righteous."﴾ [al-Saffat 37:100] Then God, the Exalted, said: ﴿So when he had withdrawn from them and what they worshipped other than God, We gave him Isaac and Jacob﴾ [Maryam 19:49]. Also, God said: ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾ [al-Saffat 37:107], and He mentioned that the ransom was for the forbearing boy whom Abraham was given good news of. He was given good news of Isaac, for God said: ﴿And We gave him good news of Isaac﴾ [al-Saffat 37:112], and here He said: ﴿a forbearing boy﴾ [al-Saffat 37:101]. That was before he married Hagar and before Ishmael was born to him. And there is nothing in the Qur'an that says he was given good news of a son except Isaac.

Those who held that it was Ishmael argued that God described him with patience, and not Isaac, in God's words: ﴿And Ishmael and Idris and Dhu al-Kifl, all of them were among the patient﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:85], and this is his patience in the sacrifice. He was described as true to his promise in God's words: ﴿Indeed, he was true to his promise﴾ [Maryam 19:54], because he promised his father from himself patience in the sacrifice and fulfilled it. Also, God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We gave him good news of Isaac, a prophet﴾ [al-Saffat 37:112], so how would He command him to sacrifice Isaac when He had promised that he would be a prophet? Also, God, the Exalted, said: ﴿So We gave her good news of Isaac, and after Isaac, Jacob﴾ [Hud 11:71]. So how would Isaac be commanded to be sacrificed before the promise regarding Jacob was fulfilled? Also, reports mention that a ram's horn was hung in the Ka'bah, which indicates that the sacrificed one was Ishmael; and had it been Isaac, the sacrifice would have taken place at Bayt al-Maqdis.

All this reasoning is not conclusive. As for their claim: How would He command him to sacrifice him when He had promised that he would be a prophet? It is possible that the meaning is: And We gave him good news of his prophethood after what had happened to him, as Ibn 'Abbas said, and it will come. Perhaps he was commanded to sacrifice Isaac after Jacob had been born to Isaac. It is said: The Qur'an does not state that Jacob was born to Isaac.

As for their claim: If the sacrificed one were Isaac, the sacrifice would have taken place at Bayt al-Maqdis, the answer to it is what Sa'id ibn Jubayr said, as previously mentioned.

Al-Zajjaj said: God knows which of them was the sacrificed one. This is a third position.

The second issue: God's words, ﴿He said: "O my son, I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you; so see what you think."﴾ Muqatil said: Abraham saw this for three consecutive nights. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: Revelation came to the messengers from God while they were awake or asleep, for the hearts of the prophets do not sleep. This is established in a hadith traced to the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "We, the company of prophets, our eyes sleep but our hearts do not sleep."

Ibn 'Abbas said: The dreams of the prophets are revelation, and he used this verse as evidence.

Al-Suddi said: When Abraham was given good news of Isaac before he was born to him, he said: "Then I shall be a sacrifice to God." It was said to him in his dream: "You have made a vow, so fulfil your vow." It is said that Abraham saw, on the night of Tarwiyah, as if someone said: "God commands you to sacrifice your son." When he woke in the morning, he reflected within himself on whether this dream was from God or from Satan, and so that day was named the Day of Tarwiyah (reflection). When the second night came, he saw the same and was told the promise, and when he woke in the morning he knew that it was from God, so that day was named the Day of 'Arafah (recognition). Then he saw the same in the third night and resolved to sacrifice him, so that day was named the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr).

It is reported that when he sacrificed him, Gabriel said: "God is greatest, God is greatest." The sacrificed one said: "There is no god but God, and God is greatest." Abraham said: "God is greatest, and praise be to God." So this remained a sunnah.

People differed about whether this matter actually took place. The people of the Sunnah said: The act of slaughter itself did not occur; rather, the command to slaughter occurred before the slaughter could take place. Had it taken place, its reversal could not be conceived. So this was a case of abrogation (naskh) before the act, because had the carrying out of the command to slaughter been completed, the ransom would not have been realised. God's words ﴿You have certainly fulfilled the vision﴾ mean: You have realised what We alerted you to; you did what was within your ability, then you were restrained when We prevented you. This is the soundest of what has been said on this subject.

Another group said: This is not something that can be abrogated in any way, because the meaning of "I slaughtered the thing" is "I cut it." They based this on the saying of Mujahid: Isaac said to Abraham: "Do not look at me, lest you show mercy to me, but turn my face toward the ground." Abraham took the knife and drew it over his throat, but it flipped over. He said to him: "What is the matter with you?" He said: "The knife has turned over." He said: "Stab me with it, stab me." Some of them said: Every time he cut a part, it healed. Others said: He found his throat to be brass, or covered with brass, and every time he wanted to cut, he found an obstacle.

All of this is possible within divine power, but it requires a sound transmission, for it is a matter that cannot be grasped by reasoning, and its only path is report. Had this happened, God would have made it clear, glorifying the rank of Ishmael and Abraham, may the blessings of God be upon them both, and it would have been more fitting to explain than the ransom.

Some said: Abraham was not commanded to perform the true slaughter, which is cutting the jugular veins and letting the blood flow. Rather, he saw that he had laid him down for slaughter, and he imagined that he had been commanded to perform the true slaughter. When he did what he had been commanded, which was laying him down, it was said to him: ﴿You have certainly fulfilled the vision.﴾ But all this lies outside the plain meaning. It cannot be supposed that the friend (Abraham) and the sacrificed one (Ishmael or Isaac) would understand from this command something that has no reality, so as to have such an imagination.

Moreover, even if these things were true, the ransom would not have been necessary.

The fourth issue: God's words ﴿so see what you think﴾. The people of Kufa, other than 'Asim, read "mādhā tūrī" with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the ra', from urriya yurī. Al-Farra' said: meaning, so see what you show (of your patience and your anxiety). Al-Zajjaj said: No one has said this except him. Rather, the scholars said: "mā dhā tushīr," that is, what your own self shows you of opinion. Abu 'Ubayd rejected "turā" and said: This can only be from seeing with the eye specifically. Abu Hatim also said likewise. Al-Nahhas said: This is a mistake, for it can come from seeing with the eye and from other than that, and it is well known: one says "I showed so-and-so the right course" and "I showed him his guidance," and this is not seeing with the eye.

The rest read "tarā," the present tense of ra'ayta. It has also been transmitted from al-Dahhak and al-A'mash as "turā," in the passive voice.

He did not say this to him in the manner of consulting about God's command; rather, he consulted him to know his patience with God's command, or so that his eye would be comforted when he saw from his son obedience in God's command.

So he said: ﴿"O my father, do what you are commanded. You will find me, if God wills, of the patient."﴾ That is, what you are commanded to do, so the preposition was omitted, as it was omitted in the line of poetry:

"I commanded you the good, so do what you were commanded."

So the verb reached the pronoun, becoming tu'maruhu, then the hā' was dropped, as in His words: ﴿And peace be upon His servants whom He chose﴾ [al-Naml 27:59], meaning those whom He chose, as previously mentioned [[See vol. 13, p. 22, first or second edition.]]. And "mā" here means "alladhī" (that which).

﴿You will find me, if God wills, of the patient.﴾ Some of the people of allusion (ishārah) said: When he made the exception by saying "if God wills," God granted him patience.

The discussion of ﴿O my father﴾ [Yusuf 12:4] has already passed, and likewise ﴿O my son﴾ [Yusuf 12:5] in the commentary on Surah Yusuf, and elsewhere [[See vol. 9, p. 121, first or second edition; and vol. 2, p. 136, second edition.]].

**Fifth:** His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When they had both submitted﴾, meaning they both yielded to the command of Allah. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them all, read "fa-lamma sallama", meaning they entrusted their affair to Allah. Ibn 'Abbas said: "They surrendered (istaslama)." Qatadah said: "One of them surrendered himself to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and the other surrendered his son." ﴿And he laid him down upon his brow﴾. Qatadah said: "He threw him down and turned his face toward the qiblah."

The answer to "lamma" (when) is omitted according to the Basrans (the grammarians of Basra). Its implied sense is: "When they both submitted and he laid him down upon his brow, We ransomed him with a ram." The Kufans (the grammarians of Kufa) said: the answer is "We called out to him," and the waw is superfluous and inserted, as in His saying: ﴿So when they took him away and agreed to put him into the depths of the well, and We inspired him﴾ [Yusuf: 15], meaning "We inspired him." Also His saying: ﴿And they, from every mound, will swarm﴾ [al-Anbiya': 96]. And "wa-iqtaraba" (and drew near) means "iqtaraba" (drew near). And His saying: ﴿Until, when they reached it and its gates were opened and its keepers said﴾ [al-Zumar: 73], meaning "said to them." Imru' al-Qays said:

"So when we crossed the courtyard of the tribe and it inclined,
with us into the valley of Khabt, the hillocky, winding..."

meaning "it inclined," and the waw is superfluous. He also said:

"Until, when your bellies have been loaded and you have seen your sons grown up,
and you have turned the back of the shield against us, and indeed the base, wicked, deceitful one..."

He meant "qalabtum" (you turned). Al-Nahhas said: the waw is among the particles of meaning, and it is not permissible for it to be superfluous.

It is reported in a khabar (report) that the one to be sacrificed said to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, when he intended to slaughter him: "O my father, tighten my bonds so that I do not thrash about; hold back your garments so that none of my blood splashes on them and your mother sees it and grieves; hasten the passage of the knife over my throat so that death may be easier for me; and turn me onto my face so that you do not look at my face and show mercy to me, and so that I do not look at the blade and panic. And when you come to my mother, convey my greetings to her." When Ibrahim, peace be upon him, drew the knife, Allah struck upon it a plate of copper, so the knife did nothing. Then he struck at his brow and cut into his nape, but the knife did nothing. That is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And he laid him down upon his brow﴾.

Ibn 'Abbas likewise said that its meaning is that he laid him on his face, and then he was called: ﴿O Ibrahim, you have fulfilled the vision﴾, so he turned and saw a ram. This was mentioned by al-Mahdawi. Its soundness has already been called into question, and the meaning is that when he (Ibrahim) had resolved upon the obligation and prepared himself for the act, this one (the son) was in the state of one who is to be slaughtered and that one (the knife) in the form of a slaughtering instrument. Both were given a place of slaughter as a ransom, and there was no passing of a knife. On this basis, abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by a later one) before the act can be conceived, as has been mentioned previously. And Allah knows best.

Al-Jawhari said: "And he laid him down upon his brow" means he threw him down, as you say "kabbahu li-wajhihi" (he overturned him onto his face). Al-Harawi said: "al-tall" means pushing and throwing down, and from it is the hadith of Abu al-Darda', may Allah be pleased with him: "And they left you for your fall (li-mattalika)," meaning for your downfall. In another hadith: "He came with a she-camel, kawma', and he tallaha," meaning he made her kneel. In a hadith: "While I was sleeping, the keys of the treasures of the earth were brought to me, and they were tullat in my hand," meaning they were placed in my hand. Ibn al-Anbari said: this means they were cast into my hand; it is said "tallaltu al-rajul" when you cast the man down. Ibn al-A'rabi said: they were poured into my hand; "al-tall" is pouring, and it is said "tall yatullu" when one pours, and "tall yatillu" (with kasra) when one falls.

I say: In Sahih Muslim, from Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was brought a drink, and he drank from it, while on his right was a boy and on his left were elders. He said to the boy: "Will you permit me to give these people (the elders) [a share]?" The boy said: "No, by Allah, I will not give up my share from you to anyone." He said: "So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) placed it (tallahu) in his hand," meaning he set it in his hand.

Some people of allusion (ahl al-ishara, the Sufi interpreters) said: Ibrahim claimed the love of Allah, then he looked at the son with love, and his Beloved did not accept a shared love. So it was said to him: "O Ibrahim, slaughter your son for My pleasure." He hastened, took the knife, laid his son down, and said: "O Allah, accept him from me for Your pleasure." Then Allah inspired him: "O Ibrahim, the aim was not the slaughter of the son; the aim was that you return your heart to Us. When you returned your heart to Us wholly, We returned your son to you."

Ka'b and others said: When Ibrahim was shown in a dream the slaughter of his son, Satan said: "By Allah, if I do not tempt the family of Ibrahim at this point, I will never tempt any of them ever." So Satan appeared to them in the form of a man, then came to the boy's mother and said: "Do you know where Ibrahim is taking your son?" She said: "No." He said: "He is taking him to slaughter him." She said: "Never! He is more compassionate toward him than that." He said: "He claims that his Lord commanded him to do so." She said: "If his Lord has commanded him to do so, then he has done well to obey his Lord."

Then he came to the boy and said: "Do you know where your father is taking you?" He said: "No." He said: "He is taking you to slaughter you." He said: "Why?" He said: "He claims that his Lord commanded him to do so." He said: "Then let him do what Allah has commanded him, hearing and obeying the command of Allah."

Then he came to Ibrahim and said: "Where are you going? By Allah, I think that Satan has come to you in your sleep and commanded you to slaughter your son." Ibrahim recognised him and said: "Get away from me, O enemy of Allah! By Allah, I will surely carry out the command of my Lord." The accursed one did not succeed in anything against them.

Ibn 'Abbas said: When Ibrahim was commanded to slaughter his son, Satan appeared to him at the Jamrat al-'Aqabah and he threw seven pebbles at him until he went away. Then he appeared to him at the middle Jamrah and he threw seven pebbles at him until he went away. Then he appeared to him at the other Jamrah and he threw seven pebbles at him until he went away. Then Ibrahim proceeded in obedience to the command of Allah, the Exalted.

There is disagreement about the place where he intended to slaughter him. It was said: in Makkah, at the Maqam. It was said: at the slaughtering place in Mina, near the pebbles with which Iblis, may Allah curse him, was stoned. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib. It is reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he slaughtered him upon the rock at the foot of Thabir in Mina. Ibn Jurayj said: He slaughtered him in al-Sham (Syria), in Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), two miles away. The first view is the more common, for it is reported in the reports that the ram's horn was hung in the Ka'bah, which indicates that he slaughtered him in Makkah. Ibn 'Abbas said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, it was indeed at the beginning of Islam, and the head of the ram was hanging by its two horns from the spout of the Ka'bah, and it had dried out." Those who said that the slaughter took place in al-Sham answered: Perhaps the head was carried from al-Sham to Makkah. And Allah knows best.

**Sixth:** His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good﴾, meaning We reward them with deliverance from hardships in this world and the Hereafter. ﴿Indeed, this was the manifest trial﴾, meaning the manifest blessing. It is said "abla-hu Allahu ibla'an wa-balaa'an" when Allah bestows a favour upon him, and it is also said "balaahu." Zuhayr said:

"May Allah reward with goodness what the two of them did for you,
so they bestowed upon you the best of the trial (bala') which tries..."

Some people claimed that he came with both dialects. Others said: rather, the second is from "balaahu, yabluuhu," meaning when one tests him, and "balaa" meaning testing is only said as "balaahu yabluuhu," and it is not said from "ibtila'" as "yabluuhu." The root of all this, from testing, is that it may be by good and evil. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And We test you with evil and good as a trial﴾ [al-Anbiya': 35]. Abu Zayd said: This is from the trial which befell him in that he should slaughter his son. He said: And this is from the disliked trial.
