This is said by the angels, glorifying Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and denouncing the worship of those who worshipped them: "And indeed, we are those who stand in ranks. And indeed, we are those who glorify [Allah]" (37:165–166). Muqatil said: these three verses were revealed while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was at Sidrat al-Muntaha (the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary). Jibril (Gabriel) held back, so the Prophet (ﷺ) said, "Do you part from me here?" He said, "I cannot advance beyond my place." Allah, the Exalted, then revealed, relating the words of the angels: "And there is none of us but has a known station" (37:164), and the verses that follow.

The Kufan grammarians' interpretation is: "And there is none of us but has a known station," meaning "there is none of us but he who has a known station," so the relative pronoun (al-mawsul, the relative word) is omitted. The Basran grammarians' interpretation is: "And there is none of us but there is an angel who has a known station," meaning a known place in worship. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Jubayr.

Ibn Abbas said: "There is not a span's width in the heavens where there is not an angel praying and glorifying [Allah]."

A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is not a place the width of a foot in the sky except that there is an angel on it, either prostrating or standing."

It is narrated from Abu Dharr that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I see what you do not see, and I hear what you do not hear. The sky has creaked, and it has the right to creak. There is no place the width of four fingers in it except that an angel is placing his forehead in prostration to Allah. By Allah, if you knew what I know, you would laugh little and weep much, and you would not enjoy women on beds, and you would go out to the high ground, crying out to Allah. I wish I were a tree that is cut down." Abu 'Isa al-Tirmidhi narrated it and said of it: "Hasan" [[The addition is from Sahih al-Tirmidhi.]] gharib (a hadith that is hasan and gharib). It is also reported through another route that Abu Dharr said: "I wish I were a tree that is cut down." It is also reported from Abu Dharr as a statement of his own (mawquf).

Qatadah said: Men and women used to pray together until this verse was revealed: "And there is none of us but has a known station." He said: So the men came forward and the women drew back.

"And indeed, we are those who stand in ranks." Al-Kalbi said: Their rows are like the rows of the people of the world on earth.

In Sahih Muslim, from Jabir ibn Samurah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came out to us while we were in the mosque and said, "Will you not form rows as the angels form rows before their Lord?" We said, "O Messenger of Allah, how do the angels form rows before their Lord?" He said, "They complete the first rows and they close up the ranks within the row."

'Umar used to say when he stood for prayer: "Straighten your rows and stand evenly, for Allah only wants you to have the guidance of the angels before their Lord," and he would recite, "And indeed, we are those who stand in ranks," then say, "Step back, O so-and-so; step forward, O so-and-so." Then he would advance and say the takbir. Its explanation has already passed in Surat al-Hijr [[See vol. 10, p. 19 onward, first or second edition.]].

Abu Malik said: People used to pray scattered, so Allah, the Exalted, revealed, "And indeed, we are those who stand in ranks," and the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded them to line up in rows.

Al-Sha'bi said: Jibril, or an angel, came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "Stand [in prayer] for nearly two-thirds of the night, or half of it, or a third of it" (cf. 73:20). "Indeed the angels pray and glorify [Allah], and there is no vacant angel in the heavens."

It was also said: meaning, "indeed we are those who stand in ranks," with our wings spread in the air, standing, waiting for what we are commanded.

It was also said: meaning, we are those who stand in ranks around the Throne.

"And indeed, we are those who glorify [Allah]," meaning those who pray. Qatadah said: It was also said: meaning those who declare Allah free of what the polytheists attribute to Him. The meaning is that they inform [the people] that they worship Allah through glorification and prayer, and that they are not the ones worshipped, nor the daughters of Allah.

It was also said: "And there is none of us but has a known station" is a statement of the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers addressing the polytheists, meaning that for each one of us and of you there is a known station in the Hereafter, which is the station of reckoning. It was also said: meaning, among us is one who has the station of fear, among us one who has the station of hope, among us one who has the station of sincerity, and among us one who has the station of gratitude, along with other stations.

I say: the more apparent view is that this refers back to the words of the angels: "And there is none of us but has a known station." And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 37, verses 167–170:

He returns to reporting the statement of the polytheists, meaning that before the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ), when they were reproached for their ignorance, they would say: "If only we had a reminder from the earlier peoples" (﴿لَوْ أَنَّ عِندَنَا ذِكْرًا مِّنَ الْأَوَّلِينَ﴾), meaning: if a prophet had been sent to us bringing a clarification of the laws (shara'i'), we would have followed him.

When "in" (inna) is lightened (mukhaffafah), it enters upon the verb and is required to be accompanied by the lam (la-), in order to distinguish between negation and affirmation. The Kufans say: "in" here carries the meaning of "ma" (not), and the lam carries the meaning of "illa" (except). It has also been said that the meaning of "if we had a reminder" is a book from the books of the prophets. ﴿لَكُنَّا عِبَادَ اللَّهِ الْمُخْلَصِينَ﴾ means: if a reminder had come to us as it came to the earlier peoples, we would have made our worship purely for God.

﴿فَكَفَرُوا بِهِ﴾ means: they disbelieved in it, that is, in the Reminder. Al-Farra' considers it to be elided (muqaddar 'ala hadhf), meaning: Muhammad (ﷺ) came to them with the Reminder, and they disbelieved in it. This is an expression of wonder at them, meaning: a prophet has indeed come to them and a book has been sent down to them containing a clarification of what they need, yet they disbelieved, and they did not fulfil what they had said.

﴿فَسَوْفَ يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: they will come to know the outcome (maghabbah) of their disbelief.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But when it descends upon their courtyard﴾, that is, the punishment. Al-Zajjaj said: the punishment of these people was by killing. The meaning of "upon their courtyard" is upon their dwelling, according to al-Suddi and others. Al-sahah and al-sahsah in the language mean the wide open space in front of a house. Al-Farra' said: "descended upon their courtyard" and "descended upon them" are the same. "Then evil is the morning of those who were warned" — that is, evil is the morning of those who were warned of the punishment. This clarifies the meaning of "when it descends upon their courtyard," meaning the Prophet ﷺ. "And turn away from them for a time" is repeated for emphasis, and likewise "and watch, and they will see" is also for emphasis.

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 37, verses 180–182:

There are four issues concerning this.

The first concerns His saying, ﴿Glory be to your Lord﴾. He (exalted is He) declared Himself free from what the polytheists attributed to Him. "Lord of Might" is in apposition (*badal*). It may also be in the accusative (*nasb*) as praise, and in the nominative (*raf'*) with the meaning "He is the Lord of Might." "What they describe" means, namely, companions and offspring. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about the meaning of "Glory be to Allah," and he said: "It is the declaration of Allah's transcendence above every evil." This has already been discussed in full in *al-Baqarah* [[See vol. 1, pp. 276 and 852 onward, second or third edition; and vol. 2, p. 76 onward, second edition.]].

The second concerns Muhammad ibn Sahnun, who was asked about the meaning of "Lord of Might." How is this permissible, given that might is one of the attributes of the Essence, while one does not say "Lord of Power" or similar expressions for His essential attributes, exalted and mighty is He? He replied: Might may be an attribute of the Essence and an attribute of Action. The attribute of the Essence is like His saying, ﴿So to Allah belongs all might﴾, while the attribute of Action is like His saying, "Lord of Might." The meaning is: Lord of the might by which creatures overpower one another, and that is among the creation of Allah, mighty and majestic is He. He said: It has been reported in the exegesis that "might" here refers to the angels. He said: Some of our scholars said: Whoever swears by the might of Allah, if he intends His might which is His attribute and then breaks the oath, he must pay the expiation (*kaffara*). If he intends that which Allah placed among His servants, there is no expiation for him.

Al-Mawardi said: "Lord of Might" may bear two meanings. One is the Owner of might. The other is the Lord of everything that gains might, whether a king or a tyrant. I say: On both meanings, there is no expiation if the swearer intended it.

The third concerns what has been transmitted from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say before concluding the prayer: "Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might," up to the end of the surah. This was mentioned by al-Tha'labi. I say: I read with the Shaykh, the Imam, the hadith scholar, the memorizer Abu 'Ali al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Amruk al-Bakri, in al-Jazira, opposite al-Mansura in the land of Egypt. He said: Al-Hurra Umm al-Mu'ayyad Zaynab bint 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hasan al-Sha'iri informed us in Nishapur on the first occasion. Abu Muhammad Isma'il ibn Abi Bakr al-Qari informed us, saying: Abu al-Hasan 'Abd al-Ghafir ibn Muhammad al-Farisi told us, saying: Abu Sahl Bishr ibn Ahmad al-Isfara'ini told us, saying: Abu Sulayman Dawud ibn al-Husayn al-Bayhaqi told us, saying: Abu Zakariyya Yahya ibn Yahya ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Tamimi al-Nishapuri told us, saying: Hushaym told us, from Abu Haroun al-'Abdi, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) more than once or twice say at the end of his prayer, or as he turned away: "Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe. And peace be upon the messengers. And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds."

Al-Mawardi said: Al-Sha'bi narrated, saying: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever would like to receive the fullest measure of reward on the Day of Resurrection, let him say at the end of his sitting, when he wishes to rise: 'Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe. And peace be upon the messengers. And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.'" This was mentioned by al-Tha'labi from the hadith of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, as a marfu' report (traced to the Prophet).

The fourth concerns His saying, ﴿And peace be upon the messengers﴾, meaning those who conveyed from Allah, exalted is He, the Oneness of God and the message. Anas said that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When you greet me, greet the messengers as well, for I am only a messenger among the messengers." It was also said: The meaning of "And peace be upon the messengers" is security granted to them by Allah, mighty and majestic is He, on the Day of the Great Terror. "And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds" means for sending the messengers as bringers of good news and warners. It was also said: It means for all that Allah has bestowed upon all creatures. And it was said: It means for the destruction of the polytheists, its evidence being His saying: ﴿So the last remnant of the people who did wrong was cut off. And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-An'am: 45]. I say: All of these are intended, and the praise encompasses them all. The meaning of "they describe" is "they lie," and the implied sense is "what they describe of falsehood." The exegesis of Surah al-Saffat is complete.
